subtopic: COMMITTEES OF THE HOUSE
COMMITTEES OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the report of the legislative committee on Bill C-273, an Act respecting political rights of public employees, in both official languages.
I believe it would benefit all Members if I presented a short explanation of the action taken by the legislative committee with respect to Bill C-273 which will enact a new public employees' political rights Act.
Bill C-273 was introduced as a Private Member's Bill by the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) and received substantial attention and support. There were two important developments prompting this interest. First, those active in political life now believe public employees should have a code of political rights along the lines recommended by the D'Avig-non report in 1979. Second, existing statutory restrictions may violate the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms enacted in 1982.
The task of the legislative committee was to balance the demand for enhanced political rights with the tradition of independence and neutrality in public employment. I believe the revision of Bill C-273 by the legislative committee has achieved this delicate balance.
The amendments respond to the advice and the recommendations brought to the committee and resulted in all-Party agreement. The revised provisions are supported by a committee membership whose mutual belief is that public employees merit all the rights of Canadian citizenship with narrow exceptions to protect the public interest. In the result, we believe the Bill commands the support of all Members of the House of Commons.

subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS-REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
HUMAN RIGHTS-REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table in both official languages the First Report of the Standing Committee on Human Rights concerning human rights behind the Iron Curtain. The report notes that the people of countries behind the Iron Curtain do not have many fundamental rights, and your Committee requests that the Government of Canada make a comprehensive response to the report.

This report is released at an important time in the East-West relationship. The Vienna follow-up meeting of the Helsinki Final Act process is still ongoing. In the Soviet Union there are signs of change reflected in the phenomena of perestroika and glasnost.

June 21, 1988
Tabling of Documents
The committee has examined the human rights situation behind the Iron Curtain and has concluded that there is still much headway to be made. The real litmus test of the genuineness of glasnost and perestroika will be seen in the degree of real change in relation to freedom of religion, the rights of national minorities, and immigration for family reunification.

MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: FUNDING OF SEWER AND WATER INFRASTRUCTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to lend support to the request made by the Canadian Federation of Municipalities. It has made a request to the Government of Canada to cost share with the provincial Governments and municipalities to provide needed expenditures for the basic infrastructure that is required throughout this country, namely, sewer and water.
June 21, 1988

There are a number of municipalities, both large and small, which are in need of cost sharing with the provinces and the Government of Canada to provide these necessary services. In my own province, communities such as Halifax, Dartmouth, smaller communities such as Sydney, New Waterford, and the municipality of the County of Cape Breton, are all in need of government funding to provide these necessities which have become very, very important over the last number of years.
Members should recognize, particularly government Members, that this request, if fortified by the Government of Canada, would not only provide necessary services to those small and large communities, but would provide needed employment in many of those communities. It would also add to the environmental impact throughout the country.
I believe this to be a positive request and I would hope the Government through its Members would see the light of day and pass sufficient programs to provide the necessary water and sewer services across the country.

Mr. Speaker, the voters of Lac-Saint-Jean yesterday decided massively in favour of Conservative Lucien Bouchard. He obtained 16,986 votes, or 55 per cent, compared to 10,726 votes for the Liberal candidate of Leader John Turner.
The big loser in this election is the NDP candidate of Leader Ed Broadbent, who did not manage to get 3,000 votes.
The Prime Minister ctf Canada (Mr. Mulroney) said last night, "It is an impressive victory. Lucien Bouchard is an outstanding Quebecer and Canadian, who will do great service for Canadian unity."
Mr. Speaker, we Conservatives of Quebec are all proud of this great victory in Lac-Saint-Jean.
Mr. Speaker, Lucien Bouchard has already started his work as Member of Parliament for Lac-Saint-Jean. He is a man of action. Congratulations, Lucien Bouchard!

subtopic: SERVICE CHARGES-ROYAL BANK'S DEDUCTION FOR COMPUTER SERVICES
SERVICE CHARGES-ROYAL BANK'S DEDUCTION FOR COMPUTER SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic
Affairs tabled its report on bank service charges, my office has been inundated with complaints about bank service charges. What I have decided to do, starting today, is to read into the record letters from Canadians complaining about bank service charges.
Dear Sir;
I noticed on TV news this morning an item on excessive bank charges. Yours was the only name I picked up, other than that of Robert McIntosh, who is paid to support excessive bank charges.
I too am a low income person and have little money in my account with the Royal Bank. To my astonishment they deducted $20. When I asked why, the manager informed me it was for computer services. I hadn't used any computer services at all, except my account number is likely on it. I had no way to fight it. It was just done out of the blue and without any notice to me about it. I felt I was robbed. I was robbed. If one is of low economic resources then it seems we are ripe for picking.
Am enclosing a zerox of deduction.
It is signed Mrs. Georgenna Ferguson, Calgary, Alberta.

subtopic: EFFECT OF PART-TIME JOBS ON WELFARE PAYMENTS
EFFECT OF PART-TIME JOBS ON WELFARE PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hundreds of would be employers are frustrated and angry when a Canadian refuses a part-time job offer because acceptance would mean their welfare or UIC would be cut off and they would be left high and dry. Why are government policies not flexible enough to permit such people to work part-time without cutting off their entire income? If such Canadians could benefit by a reduction of less than the amount they would earn, a recipient would be ahead and the Government's expenditures would be reduced.
Present policies force Canadians to stay on welfare and UIC as long as their payments permit. No wonder the jobs offered by 42 per cent of the firms belonging to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business remain unfilled.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to mourn the passing of a great Quebecer and Canadian, a scientist, humanitarian and great communicator, Fernand Seguin. Mr. Seguin gave us years of enthusiastic service. Who does not remember his program Le sel de la semainel For some of us, the world of science was mysterious and inaccessible, but Mr. Seguin opened the doors for us; he let us into the world of scientists, to understand their ideas and their discussions, even what they were doing. He helped us to

June 21, 1988
explore our own ideas as well and to ponder our origins and our future in a changing world.
In these times when science occupies an important place, both for our comfort and for our security, he gave us a thirst for knowledge.
To his wife and family, I offer my sincerest condolences. It is with great regret that, on behalf of all Quebecers and Canadians, I say to him, "Farewell and thanks."

subtopic: WELFARE RECIPIENTS HIRING PROGRAM
WELFARE RECIPIENTS HIRING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to have this opportunity to mention a very useful program initiated by this Government to help welfare recipients re-enter the labour market. This job development program enables selected employers to receive federal assistance in hiring workers, which is an essential adjunct to the development of their enterprise and at the same time provides welfare recipients with a substantial salary, increased training and an excellent opportunity for social reintegration.
Mr. Speaker, I may point out here in the House that under this innovative program, seven businesses and organizations in my riding will be offering twenty-five new jobs to welfare recipients, thanks to a contribution of $201,478. It is because Canadians want us to maintain these initiatives that they continue to trust and support us.

subtopic: EFFECT OF SUBSIDIES ON GRAIN HANDLERS
EFFECT OF SUBSIDIES ON GRAIN HANDLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the layoff of more than one-third of Thunder Bay's grain handlers earlier this month has renewed concern about wheat exports through the St. Lawrence Seaway.
As many as 600 of Thunder Bay's 1,800 elevator workers lost seniority rights during the slow years 1984-85 and 198586. Employment recovered during the record 1986-87 year, and reached 1,300 this spring.
Earlier than usual layoffs this month have combined with very dry prairie weather to arouse fear of crop failure and a slow fall in the elevators. The real problem, however, is a glut of wheat in our traditional markets resulting from subsidies.
Little more than a decade ago the European Economic Community had a grain shortfall of 24 million tonnes. By 1986
high farm support prices had transformed this into a surplus of 14 million tonnes.
The Economic Summit is considering the problem of agricultural subsidies. The European Economic Community spends 80 per cent of its budget on such subsidies.
It is time Governments find other means of maintaining farm incomes in Europe and the U.S. too, than those that lead to hardship for western farmers and Thunder Bay grain handlers.

Mr. Speaker, politicos across Canada are wiping at least some egg off their respective faces today as the tight race in yesterday's byelection in the constituency of Lac-Saint-Jean never did materialize. The Secretary of State easily outdistanced his rivals and sent the Hon. Leaders of the Opposition back to the old drawing-board.
The Secretary of State's reputation, ability, and resources should not have been taken lightly. He is an able campaigner who employed a unique system of political contributions- 1,500 contributors, no union contributions, no corporate contributions, just the support of the people of Lac-Saint-Jean at the grass roots level.

Bravo, Mr. Minister! A great performance! Welcome to the House!

subtopic: PRESENCE IN CANADA OF RENAMO INFORMATION CHIEF
PRESENCE IN CANADA OF RENAMO INFORMATION CHIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, news that Mr. Francisco Nota Moises, Information Chief of the Mozambican rebel organization Renamo, has been granted asylum in Canada should be of concern to all Canadians. Mr. Moises' presence in Canada once again demonstrates the glaring deficiencies in Canada's immigration and security system.
To allow such an individual into this country, particularly when Mr. Moises' activities for Renamo were widely know, is completely unacceptable. It is obviously high time that the Government got its act together.
June 21, 1988

In addition, Renamo is a particularly reprehensible group that has been accused of killing 100,000 Mozambican civilians in the last two years, and is responsible for a systematic campaign of rape, torture, and terror in Mozambique.
Renamo is also a proxy army for South Africa in its efforts to destabilize the front line States, particularly Mozambique and its critical alternate railway to the Indian Ocean.
Canada has a policy of support for the front line States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) would do well to clear this issue up at once lest his position of support for the front line States be made into a laughing-stock.

subtopic: FORMER MINISTER'S POLICIES
FORMER MINISTER'S POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the former Minister of Communications understood that to develop strong Canadian cultural industries strong legislative measures were needed. He understood that money was not a substitute for policy. It was in that spirit that he introduced the Baie Comeau book publishing policy. He recognized that it was essential that there be Canadian control of publishing.
His film industry task force recommended that there be 100 per cent Canadian control of film distribution and that an end be put to vertical integration between film distributors and film exhibitors.
It is regrettable that the Mulroney-Reagan deal trade has changed those well-founded Canadian objectives. It is time the close encounters this Government has with the Americans become close encounters of another kind. It is too bad that the former Communications Minister isn't still writing the film policy script, for he saw the big picture. His successor is being directed frame by frame by Jack Valenti. As a result, Canada's film industry is being left on the cutting room floor. It's a sham and a shame.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, voters in Lac-Saint-Jean elected the Secretary of State, Lucien Bouchard, with a strong majority. This warm, intelligent and sincere gentleman will, together with his colleagues, continue to defend the interests of Quebec. This election is a great victory for the great team of Brian Mulroney who is putting
down strong roots in Quebec and is showing great leadership on issues that are extremely important to this country. We are delighted with the support we received from all sides yesterday, both politically and financially.
Yesterday, Broadbent's NDP candidate lost his deposit, Mr. Speaker. The NDP is seeing its hopes fade away in Quebec, and after being the great loser in the federal election, yesterday it was completely swept off the map in two provincial byelections in Quebec.
As for the federal Liberals, I say to their leader, whose leadership is still being questioned by twenty-two of his Members in the House: Keep dragging your feet on issues that are of great importance to this country: Meech Lake and free trade. I would invite Mr. Turner to come to the boundary of my riding, at Sainte-Marie de Beauce, to tell the people he intends to tear up the free trade agreement!

subtopic: WINNIPEG-NEED FOR FEDERAL FUNDING
WINNIPEG-NEED FOR FEDERAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Winnipeg there is a program called the Core Area Initiative which is funded by all three levels of government, civic, provincial, and federal. This program has been very effective in funding local community groups and community development activities.
Now with a Conservative Government in office it is dragging its heels with regard to the funding of those local groups. The very existence of some of those groups is threatened. They have been waiting for a decision on their funding since last January, and they need the Government to get off its backside and approve the applications for funding. Some of the groups, for example, the Chilean Information Centre and the Native Youth Centre, do good work in the community and they need the Government to make some decisions and allocate the money.
Do we have to call a by-election in Winnipeg in order to get these groups funded?

Mr. Speaker, in 1984, our party, the present Government, had a great plan: to create jobs and reduce unemployment. This plan was based on some key ideas and principles: national reconciliation-i.e., good

June 21, 1988

relations with the provinces-, strengthening international relations, making our country safer through a stronger national defence. So it is no accident that 1,300,000 new jobs were created. Nor is it any accident that the people of Lac-Saint-Jean yesterday voted for the Conservative Government-it is no accident that they elected Lucien Bouchard. He is a very major asset, another plus for our Party, the great team now in power. He will help further improve our relations with the provinces and thereby the status of all Canadian families. subtopic: RUSSELL TOWNSHIP, ONT.-BUSINESS INCUBATOR PROPOSAL
RUSSELL TOWNSHIP, ONT.-BUSINESS INCUBATOR PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a long time the Township of Russell in my constituency has been wanting to establish a business incubator. Unfortunately, it was told recently that there was no program by which it could have a business incubator.
The Rotary Club asked me to intervene on its behalf under the same program that was used in Lac-Saint-Jean so that the community could get the business incubator.
Although no formal application has been forthcoming from my riding yet, I would expect that the funds will be rolling in anyway because, after all, no formal application was ever filled out in Lac-Saint-Jean either. If it is good for one area, then surely it is good for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.

subtopic: CLOSURE OF BOY'S $10 ACCOUNT
CLOSURE OF BOY'S $10 ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian consumers are up in arms over the unjustified service charges being imposed by banks and have now begun to voice publicly their long-standing frustration over this unacceptable situation. One case in particular brought to my attention concerns a 15-year-old boy with a small account containing $10. Without notification, the bank proceeded to levy service charges against the account and then closed it because it considered it an inactive account.
What kind of message is being sent to young people by such actions? Why should they bother to save at all when what little they can put aside is suddenly seized without notice or warning? No one should have to pay a maintenance fee on seldom used accounts. Why should consumers be charged for closing accounts or for the errors banks make?
The Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs has proposed both fair and necessary recommendations to curb bank charges. I urge the Government to take immediate action on these recommendations and to put an end to this institutionalized rip-off of consumers.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec and Canada have just lost an eminent journalist, Fernand Seguin. During his 30-year career, Mr. Seguin dominated the field of popular science.
Since television began in Canada, he was the first to initiate us to the world of science, unpretentiously and with warmth.
He was a man of vision who knew that the future would involve both communication and science and he paved the way for the excellent journalists of whom our country is so proud today.
I want us to pay him tribute today in this House.

subtopic: COMPLETION OF MATTE BOULEVARD IN BROSSARD
COMPLETION OF MATTE BOULEVARD IN BROSSARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to find out yesterday that decision 1988-R-47 of the National Transport Agency gave the City of Brossard, in my riding, permission to continue construction of Matte Boulevard in its industrial park up to the intersection of the Canadian National Railway right of way. The roads system in the industrial park will thus be greatly improved.
This NTA decision reflects the dynamism of one of the fair cities in my constituency.
Congratulations to the City Council and Mayor Georgette Lepage for their continuing tireless efforts on behalf of my beautiful riding of La Prairie.

subtopic: RAILWAYS
RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last spike was driven into the Newfoundland Railway yesterday. The final spike was driven into the coffin of the
June 21, 1988

Newfoundland Railway by this Government yesterday, June 20, 1988.
June 20 was an interesting day. There was a federal byelection with the Prime Minister throwing around taxpayers' money as if there were no tomorrow. As well, the International Economic Summit was taking place in Toronto. I am sure that other Members of the House will also be concerned about this issue.
We have learned that under the old British Naturalization Act Canadian women who married men who were not British subjects prior to 1947 automatically lost their Canadian citizenship. That is a horrendous situation which obviously needs to be changed.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, what can women do who find themselves in this situation? In addition, under the current statute, Part III, the Act of 1977, women who lost their Canadian status, such as the people to whom the Hon. Member referred, can have their citizenship restored simply by advising of their intention to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and my colleagues in the House of Commons for this time. I regret to have to inform the House of the tragic death of six officers in an accidental explosion at Canadian Forces Base Chilliwack, British Columbia. Three other officers were injured in this same accident.
I am sure I speak for all Members of this House as I extend sympathy to the parents, families, and friends of these Canadian Forces members. I share their sense of profound loss in the wake of this terrible tragedy.
At this point there would appear to be nothing which would suggest a relationship to two other recent accidents, the accidental detonation of an old artillery round at CFB Valcartier, Quebec, and misdirected mortar rounds at CFB Gagetown, New Brunswick. These two accidents are being addressed in separate boards of inquiry. However, a new board of inquiry is being convened to investigate thoroughly this most recent tragic loss of life. Results of all three inquiries will be made public on completion.
General Paul Manson, Chief of the Defence Staff, has asked Major General Frederick Sutherland, Chief of Personnel Development, to be his personal envoy. General Sutherland
June 21, 1988

will immediately proceed to Chilliwack to represent General Manson as the families and colleagues of these service people recover from this tragic loss.
This latest tragedy is a vivid reminder of the dangers that are present for the men and women who volunteer and train to defend Canada and Canadians. I still hold the conviction that our safety procedures are the best in the world. However, I am directing the Department of National Defence to review these procedures to ensure their continuing refinement in meeting the challenges which increasing technology places on our training system.
I know that all Members of the House and all members of the Canadian Forces join with me in extending sincere condolences to the families of those service people who were killed or injured in this tragic incident.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade) moved
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-130, an Act to implement the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a distinct pleasure and privilege, as well as a duty, to rise to introduce this Bill on second reading. It is just as it says, "an Act to implement the Free

Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America". It has 153 clauses and 123 pages. The Bill is devoted to doing just that, to implementing the free trade agreement.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that in reaching this stage the negotiations commenced between Canada and the United States to reach this agreement on June 17, 1986, just over two years ago. On October 4, 1987 the elements of this agreement were agreed to by the two contracting parties, the United States and ourselves, and the agreement was signed by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and by the President of the United States of America on January 3, 1988.
We are not dealing with a piece of legislation or an agreement that contains any unknowns or any major changes to what we have all understood since the agreement was signed, the elements agreed to, and the legal text made available. It has been a two-year process.
I want also just to point out that in the Senate, in the Upper House, in June of 1978 there was a report-of course, the majority was Liberal then, just as it is Liberal now-that urged the Government to consider seriously the option of bilateral free trade. We are not introducing something new or strange or startling to the Senate when our legislation reaches the Senate.
I want to point out that in March, 1982 a Senate committee, chaired by the same chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee as is now chairing that committee, recommended bilateral trade with the United States and dismissed fears about any possible reduction in sovereignty that might be suffered in Canada as a result of such a free trade agreement. I think the same Senator, Senator George Van Roggen, is still the Chairman of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee. These were his recommendations and those of the committee in March of 1982.
I might even point out that on November 5, 1987 a Senate Committee began to study the free trade situation with an order of reference from November to March of 1989. They have met to date 34 times and have heard 71 witnesses. This agreement is not a strange document or an obscure document to our Upper House. There were four days' debate on the elements of the agreement as a result of a motion of Senator Gigantes on October 29, 1987.
As a matter of fact, on May 4, 1988 the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs of the Senate reported on constitutional jurisdiction pertaining to the free trade agreement and concluded that the Government of Canada had the legislative and constitutional jurisdiction to carry out, to implement, and to pass into law that agreement here in Canada, under our trade and commerce powers, interprovincial and international, as well as other powers given to the Government of Canada by the BNA Act. It was in the House of Commons, that this agreement and this subject has had great consideration.
June 21, 1988
On October 26, 1987 the House committee started hearings on the elements of the agreement. They heard 158 witnesses in 24 days of testimony. They reported on December 15, 1987. There have been six Opposition Days devoted to this subject in this House, including September 23, 1987 when the Leader of the New Democratic Party proposed that Canada walk away-a very peculiar proposal-from the trade deal.
On October 26, 1987 the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) proposed that the agreement be torn up. It was the most feeble, the silliest, the most supercilious, the most damaging suggestion ever made by the Leader of a national Party in our history, that a major international agreement be torn up, and that he, if he got the chance himself, would tear it up, it is shows such an abysmal lack of information about this agreement. The hon. gentleman wants to engage in a feat of strength, attempting to tear up this Bill and all additions to it, which have a height of about this; Charles Atlas himself could not tear it up.
The facts are that if this agreement is implemented by this Parliament and by the U.S. Congress, under the terms of the agreement only a six-month notice needs to be given by either one of the contracting parties to result in the cancellation and the ending of the agreement anyway.
If the hon. gentleman, God forbid, is ever in a position to carry out his threats, he won't have to tear it up; he will just give a six-month notice, and of course the American President will give him a one-year notice under the terms of the U.S. Auto Pact that he is terminating the U.S. Auto Pact.
It will be a pretty close race to see who tears up what the quickest if either one of these "tear them up kids" gets into power in the next election, which is highly unlikely.
That is just some background, Mr. Speaker, to show you we are not dealing here with something new, something of first impression, something that has to be looked at in great detail for a great length of time. As a matter of fact, in getting to this position we have had day after day of negative obstructionism on behalf of the New Democratic Party, in a display of antidemocratic action carried to ludicrous extremes.
With the start of second reading today our country and our citizens move one step closer to the economic benefits that we will realize through this more secure and enhanced access to the largest market in the world, which is the U.S. market.
We are acting in the national interest, as is shown by the broad degree of provincial-government support-we have eight of the ten provinces-and public support for this free trade agreement across the country. The results of carrying this agreement into effect will be, over time, lower consumer prices, additional new jobs, real income gains realized in each region of the country.
This is one of the few pieces of legislation where we can say that every region of the country is going to benefit, Mr. Speaker, as a direct result of this agreement. There have been studies by the Department of Finance. There have been studies
June 21, 1988

by the Howe Institute. There have been studies by a western group by the name of the Canada West Foundation. Independent institute after institute have studied the agreement, and all have come to the same kind of conclusions.
I won't go into the details, Mr. Speaker, of all of that. There has been great detail in all of these studies.
Business investment will go up. Canadian exports will increase. Our total Canadian manufacturing output will increase. There will be a net gain of jobs by Canadians.
I am not going to engage in the debate on how great a net gain-is it 120,000, is it 180,000, or whatever? Everyone is agreed that there is going to be a net gain in new Canadian jobs in the next two years as a result of this action that we are starting to take today. This is confirmed, of course, by studies made by the Economic Council of Canada.
What we are doing in this Bill is approving the agreement and amending such Canadian laws as are necessary to meet our obligations under the agreement.
As an example, Mr. Speaker, the Special Import Measures Act is amended to provide for binding dispute settlement in countervail and anti-dumping cases. In all, 27 federal statutes are amended.
To implement the free trade agreement only one change is needed that normally comes under provincial jurisdiction, namely, the listings and mark-ups for American wine and liquor. The Government of Canada continues to hope that those provinces whose wine and liquor practices do not conform to the agreement will make this needed change themselves.
Of course the Province of Quebec has made it plain that they, for their part, will do this, that they intend to do this, and that they are going to do it.
We will only need to use any powers which we ask the House to give us in Clause 6 or Clause 9 of the agreement if a province absolutely refuses to make any change in listings, mark-up practices, and the like. This would not only be contrary to The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement but has already been found contrary, to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade which the opposition Parties say they support as they believe in the multilateral trading system. If that is the case, I hope they will urge the Province of Ontario to observe the finding of the GATT panel that their practices with respect to mark-ups, listings, and the like for wines and liquors are contrary to the GATT and have to be changed.
We will only act in that area if the province itself refuses to act. We have been told, of course, by the Province of Ontario that it will refuse. I hope that it is ready to reconsider that.
The Bill provides for the making of federal regulations to bring listings and mark-ups for wine and liquor into conformity with the free trade agreement if this is necessary in order to
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
implement fully the agreement by December 31, 1988. We are confident that this is within the power of the federal Parliament. We are prepared to put it to the test if anyone wishes to. The judiciary will settle these disagreements if they cannot be settled by the parties to them.
Negotiation of the agreement involved the most extensive consultations for any international trade agreement in Canadian history. In addition to the listing I have already given you, Mr. Speaker, there were quarterly meetings of First Ministers and over 150 meetings between federal and provincial representatives over this two-year period.
Let us compare that with the negotiations of the Auto Pact about which we hear so much. None of that took place in those negotiations, and the NDP adherents to the union movement opposed it for the most part, of course, although they now support the status quo. They want no change in anything.
Let us consider the situation in 1946 when MacKenzie King, then Prime Minister, had free trade negotiated with the United States in dead secrecy for months. No one in the Cabinet was privy to these negotiations, only MacKenzie King and the officials he appointed. Finally he consulted about the free trade deal which he had by then just about concluded with the U.S. Who did he consult with? I am told he consulted with his mother and she had been dead for something like 20 years. That was the only consultation which took place before MacKenzie King decided against free trade with the United States. Having initiated the negotiations and having had them conducted for six or eight months in total secrecy, he decided he was not going to go ahead with it.
We have consulted closely with the provinces in negotiating this agreement. My colleague, the President of Treasury Board (Miss Carney), with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) coming in at the end, and Simon Reisman did a great job for Canada. They along with Mr. Gordon Ritchie, the Deputy Ambassador, negotiated the agreement on which we are going to work co-operatively with the provinces to implement and administer. I have written to the premiers outlining how we propose to do that.
Parliament now has this Bill before it. Parliament has the right to debate this legislation and also has the right, after due deliberation, to decide on it. The minority in Parliament cannot deny that right to the majority.

I have described the process and said that we have now had the full legal text since last December. The Bill contains no surprises. It sets out in legal language the obligations set out in the agreement.
The Bill before us now has one central issue. We have to decide one main point: do we approve the free trade agreement and therefore want to implement all of the obligations of the free trade agreement, or do we reject the agreement? This is not a case in which Parliament can pick and choose among

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
pieces of the Bill. You're either for it or against it. We're for it, and we're going to put that to the Canadian people this year or next year. Those who are against it can creep out of their corners into the open and we will see who has the popular side of this argument. You can vote yes to the free trade agreement or no to the free trade agreement, but you cannot continue weaseling. You cannot say you are for free trade but against this agreement. You're for it or against it. You have a backbone or you haven't. You have to stand up and be counted.
Why is free trade with the U.S. so important to Canada? Why should we be concerned about the rules of the game for our exports to the U.S.? Our trade figures tell the story. We are one of the most export oriented countries in the industrialized world. About 25 per cent of our wealth, our GNP, and more than three million jobs arise from exports.
In 1987, 76 per cent of those exports, over $90 billion worth, went to the United States. That is why we are introducing this legislation today. That is why we want to save the Canadian people and give them an assured future by assuring that market in the United States. If anything goes wrong with our trade relationship with the United States, we stand to lose 25 per cent of our wealth.
I want hon. gentlemen opposite to explain that to the Canadian public when they tell them why they are against this agreement. They want to endanger one-quarter of all the wealth generated in Canada every year with their weaseling ways and silly questions in the House every day. They ask about what this Congressman and that Senator have been introducing when the only protection Canadians have against that is before them now. They want to sabotage that even though every day they pretend to be concerned about the protectionism in the U.S., yet they vote against the only protection we have against the very menaces they bring up every day.
All provinces depend heavily on exports to the U.S. In Atlantic Canada over two-thirds of exports went to the U.S. in 1986; 65 per cent in Newfoundland, to a high of 71 per cent in Nova Scotia. In Quebec 76 per cent of all exports went to the U.S., $2,280 per capita or over 13 per cent of its GDP. In British Columbia 46 per cent of exports went to the U.S., $7.2 billion worth or $2,471 per capita. In the prairie provinces 63 per cent of exports went to the U.S.; 44 per cent of Saskatchewan's, 56 per cent of Manitoba's, and 73 per cent of Alberta's, with an average per capita value of $2,782.
Note well, Mr. Speaker, that in Ontario 89 per cent of exports went to the U.S., $5,646 for each person in Ontario, accounting for over 27 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product of Ontario. Of all the wealth generated in Ontario every year, over a quarter of it, 27 per cent, comes from exports to the U.S. It is the Government of this province which is against the free trade agreement, which wanted to sabotage it by not agreeing to the wine and liquor listing changes and by other
patterns of conduct we have seen. That is completely inexplicable from the province which has the most to gain from this agreement.
Continued access to the U.S. market for what we produce in all parts of Canada is critical. Newfoundland plus P.E.I. plus Nova Scotia plus New Brunswick plus Quebec plus Ontario and Manitoba plus Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, plus free trade with the United States will make for a more prosperous Canada. I invite Hon. Members sitting opposite to realize that today, to join us in supporting this Bill, and to whistle it through without any more hesitation or attempts at sabotage.
What threatens this prosperity? It is threatened by U.S. protectionism. The people who work in our resource industries know about U.S. protectionism from the safeguard actions against cedar shakes and shingles and the countervail case against softwood lumber. American trade lawyers believe that both the safeguards actions on shakes and shingles and the softwood lumber countervail cases would have been decided differently had the free trade agreement been in place. Better still, the U.S. sponsors of those trade actions might well have been discouraged from bringing those trade actions in the first place had we had The Canada-U.S. FT A.
Therefore, one form which U.S. protectionism can take is politically inspired distortion of trade remedy law. Another form is direct limitation of trade as proposed in earlier versions of the U.S. omnibus trade bill which I do not have time to go into now. That, of course, is on the boards again with some changes and will have to be dealt with if it becomes law. If it becomes law, the free trade agreement will be more crucial than ever to shielding Canada from recurrent American protectionism.
As our ambassador to Washington, Allan Gotlieb, who has done a splendid job, has said:
(The FTA) is intended to address deep and persistent protectionist forces at work in the United States.
To counter the influence of declining industries in the U.S. system, it encourages long-term solutions rather than short- term fixes.
We are after long term solutions here. I congratulate Ambassador Gotlieb. He has done a splendid five year's work for his country, in the highest traditions of the Canadian diplomatic service. A grateful House of Commons and a grateful public should make sure that is realized.
This agreement is about long term solutions based on reciprocal principles, not raw political power, to give Canadian businesses secure access to the U.S. market. We cannot base it on raw political power because we do not have it. It must be based on reciprocal principles. The threat of American protectionism is one reason for free trade.
Another reason, just as important, is to reduce existing trade barriers so that we create new opportunities for Canadian
June 21, 1988

industry. That is why we are having a conference in Saskatoon today. That is why there will be 17 more between now and the middle of July, so that Canadians will learn what the new opportunities are for Canadian business in the United States under The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. What is why our trade commissioners and our personnel will be there.
We are doing studies to develop where the opportunities will be under this new regime. We must tell Canadian businesses, including small, large and medium, and any other Canadian who is interested, how to take advantage of those opportunities. What is the good of creating new opportunities for Canadian business if we do not then tell Canadian business where the opportunities lie? That is why we are spending what is in my opinion a puny sum of $10 million, to make sure they understand where those opportunities are. All Members of the House are invited to St. John's on July 6. We will show you how to put on a free trade seminar.
This is important for our resource industries because tariffs have been quite prejudicial to our ability to process raw materials here. This was testified to by Mr. William MacNess who is now Dean of the Faculty of Management of the University of Manitoba. He points out that we are allowed to ship raw resources duty free but the more value one adds the higher the tariffs.
In energy, forest products and metals, the American tariff system encourages Canadians to sell their raw resources for refining there, then buy them back in the finished form. While about 80 per cent of our exports enter the U.S. duty-free, scores of products face a mark-up high enough to make them uncompetitive. We are now making the other 20 per cent of Canada's exports competitive in the United States.
The fishery is another industry which will adapt to the new structure like a duck to water. The duty on processed seafood like fish sticks, prepared meals and other value added products, ranges from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. That is why Vic Young, President of Fisheries Products International, said:
At the moment Canadian seafood companies have been forced through a series of trade barriers to build secondary processing plants in the United States to add value to Canadian fish products. With the reduction of tariffs on such products over the next several years, there is little doubt that we will see a growth in the market for Canadian fish products and an increase in the production of these products in Atlantic Canada.
In other words, free trade will mean an increase in employment opportunities in the Atlantic Canada fishery. That is why the Atlantic Provinces support this, with the exception of Premier Ghiz of Prince Edward Island who apparently is fixated with the energy thesis he did some years ago, and supports the old national energy policy.
The third major reason for the free trade agreement is the positive effect of our having secure access to a combined North American market of almost 275 million people. We are the only major industrialized country in the world that does not have secure access to a market of at least 100 million people. We cannot depend on our own small Canadian domestic
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
market of 25 million or 26 million people if we are going to have growth and diversification of manufacturing services and technology.
Greater specialization with longer, lower cost production runs will strengthen our position in our own market, the U.S. market and in global markets. That is why I expect the hon. gentleman to have a conversion today when he finishes listening to me.
Those who say Canada should choose the Pacific Rim or Europe instead of the U.S. as our target market are wrong. We do not have to choose one over the other. That is why the Liberal policy is so silly, stupid, supine and ignorant of all the lessons of the past. We do not have to choose. There was the pitiful Liberal alternative last week. Now they are not going to have a free trade agreement with the U.S. at all. As the Economic Council of Canada has stated:
Many believe that freer trade and expanded trade with the United States
precludes expanded trade with other countries. There is no logical basis for this
view. In fact, expansion of our export sector to serve U.S. customers could well
facilitate the economies of scale needed to reach more distant markets.
In other words, free trade with the United States will help Canadian business reach the Pacific Rim and European markets. It will help attract more investment in Canadian facilities to serve the North American market, because with our agreement, clear access to the American market does not mean having to locate in the United States. One can locate here in Canada and investment will give similar access. This is critical in investment decisions where the target is the North American market, not not just the Canadian market.
We are not putting all our eggs in one basket. In 1985 we started two sets of trade negotiations, bilaterally with the United States, a success, and multilaterally under the GATT. We are still in that process. The mid term conference will be held in Montreal in December. We want to achieve new trade opportunities for Canadians both bilaterally and multilaterally-
The Liberal Opposition said that we should have confined the trade initiatives to the multilateral trade negotiations. That is a senseless statement. Even if everything goes wonderfully in the multilateral trade negotiations, and it is not, can we afford to wait the years needed to complete those negotiations to find out? What if the multilateral trade negotiations founder on the issue of agricultural subsidies or access for manufactured goods to the Japanese market? How then will we be helping our trade relations with the United States?
I remind the House that every concession granted by the U.S. to Canada in the multilateral negotiations would have to be paid for by Canada but would then be extended by the U.S. to all other countries. There is no realistic prospect that the multilateral trade negotiations could have given rise to the comprehensive scope of our bilateral agreement with the United States.
Furthermore, the free trade agreement strengthens our position vis-a-vis other countries within the multilateral trade

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
negotiations. With access secure to our major market in the United States, we can turn our full attention to bringing down barriers erected by other important trading partners like Europe, Japan and newly developed countries on the Pacific Rim.
We do not know what will be the results of the multilateral trade negotiations for several more years. We have the results of the Canada-U.S. negotiations before us today for the approval of Parliament. The best thing Hon. Members could do for this country is to pass this today and not wait for any further obstruction or delay.
The question Canadians should be asking is: Are we better off with or without the free trade agreement? The answer from Canadian business, the people who will have to compete, is clear. Small business representatives support the free trade agreement. Big business supports the free trade agreement. Resource producers support the free trade agreement. Manufacturers support the free trade agreement. Almost everyone in Canada who produces and exports supports the free trade agreement. Is there any need for any other character witnesses to the free trade agreement? Of course not.
There are those industries and individuals who will have to adjust to the increased competition from the United States. In addition to the phasing in of tariff reductions, in many cases over 10 years, there will be a complete array of programs to assist them in this adjustment. Many of those programs exist within the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion and the Department of Employment and Immigration. For particular groups like grape growers and wine producers, a special adjustment program will be announced soon. To ensure that adjustment needs are met, an advisory council on adjustment was appointed, headed by Mr. de Grandpre, with business, labour and academic representatives to ensure that no gaps or inequities remain in that adjustment picture.
Over all, here is what Donald Macdonald, former Liberal Minister of Finance and Chairman of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economy, had to say:
The free trade pact... is the beginning of a golden era for Canadian
businesses and workers... Canadian businesses and workers now have an
opportunity to crack the huge U.S. market, free from the protectionism other
world traders will confront.
Donald Macdonald is a patriotic Canadian citizen. He said he is not going to run for the Liberal Party in the next election, he is not going to support it, because of its twisted policy of being against this vital, central economic policy we are asking the House to approve today.
Another patriotic Liberal, of course, is Mr. Gerald Regan, former Premier of Nova Scotia, former Minister for International Trade. He said in an interview on April 10, 1988, with CTV-CJOH, and I refer to page 12 of that interview: "There is a large amount of support for free trade at all levels of the Liberal Party". He referred specifically to Ed Lumley, Don
Macdonald, Don Johnston, those people who held economic portfolios and responsibility, and people like Dr. Evans, who was a Parliamentary Secretary. They are all supportive of the free trade. In other words, the people in the Liberal Party who knew anything are for free trade. The no-nothings left, the remnants left in the House, are against it. What a testimony to the situation.
Mr. Regan was asked: "If you were a Maritime Premier again, you would be for it?" Gerry Regan, Premier of Nova Scotia for seven or eight years, answered: "Whole heartedly. I think it is the best way of combating regional economic disparity that I can think of because Nova Scotia can do very, very well in that sort of regime". That is the kind of testimonial we have for the free trade agreement. Not just from the scared or the ideological, or from those who have a bitter desire to get back into power or edge somebody else out, but from the people who are now in the position to be impartial and objective.
What about free trade with respect to the New Democratic Party? The Liberals say they want to tear it up. The New Democratic Party wants to tear it down. Why? For ideological reasons. The NDP is against changes in the status quo. The New Democrats are now the fat cats of the status quo and we Progressive Conservatives are the revolutionaries of Canada.
The New Democrats oppose free trade. They want Canadian industries to displace imports in our domestic market, a form of protectionism that would make Canada into an economic backwater producing over priced and out-of-date goods. The New Democrats do not recognize the creation dynamism of entrepreneurship in open markets. Their thinking is the thinking of Clement Attlee of 1945. That is where they are, back 43 years ago, struggling to come out of World War II. That is where their minds are.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party represents the district of Oshawa. He is fat cat No. 1. No unemployment, $8 billion in U.S. money invested in Oshawa by General Motors over the last 10 years. He is satisfied, but he does not want to let those benefits go to other Canadians. It is all right in Ontario, but forget it in Alberta, forget it in Quebec and forget it in Newfoundland. What is good for the Oshawa goose is no good for the Canadian gander. That is the slogan of the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party from Oshawa.
The Liberals said they favour free trade, but they oppose this agreement. They now say they are against any agreement. What is the reason? One of the things they say is that we did not achieve a complete exemption from U.S. trade remedy law. That is like saying that you married someone and you are going to tear her up because she did not turn out to be completely perfect. I am one of the few lucky enough to have married a woman who is completely perfect, but from what I have seen, that is not the experience of most. Are we to boot them out, kick them out, have nothing to do with them, because they are not perfection? The argument that the Liberals will be against the FT A because it is not perfect really

June 21, 1988
does not ring too well. Nothing in life is perfect, Mr. Speaker, believe me. Nothing is perfect. Not even being Minister for International Trade is perfection. Frankly, I am getting a bit fed up with it.

If Congress proceeds with a new Trade Law against the recommendation of that commission, it applies to Canada only if we are specifically named in the legislation. Otherwise it applies to the rest of the world and not Canada. That is a great step forward.
The second dispute settlement mechanism relates to the application of the rules for trade in specific cases. A Canada-U.S. panel will give fully binding rulings on the application of trade law for countervail, anti-dumping and safeguard cases. What is giving us the trouble is the unfair application of countervail law, not just the content of the law itself. Mr. Speaker, listening to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) reminds me of the old saying that when one is in a fight with a skunk, remember that it only has one weapon. In that regard we should take five minutes to clear the air in the House.
The fact of the matter is that we have to ask ourselves what is the purpose of this debate. We did not find out from the Minister. He was too busy tripping over his tongue to really tell us what the Conservative Party is attempting to achieve in what we all admit is a very historic, very important, very crucial debate in the House of Commons.
The Minister for International Trade ended off his remarks with a quote from Mr. Laurier. I would like to begin my remarks with another from a more thoughtful Leader of our Party, Mr. Edward Blake, who wrote to his constituents-I see that the Minister does not want to listen to the other side of the case, unfortunately.
In 1891 Mr. Blake wrote to his constituents irt West Durham the following words:
Whatever you or I may think on-whether we like or dislike, believe or
disbelieve in political union, must we not agree that the subject is one of great
moment, towards the practical settlement of which we should take no serious
step without reflection, or in ignorance of what we are doing?
He said:
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Assuming that-free trade with the States, best describes commercial union, may and ought to come, I believe that it can and should come only as an incident, or at any rate as well-understood precursor of political, union for which, indeed, we should be able to make better terms before than after the surrender of our commercial independence.
Then so believing-believing that the decision of the trade question involves that of the Constitution issue, for which we are unprepared and with which you do not even conceive yourselves to be deciding-how can I properly recommend you how to decide of commercial union?
In 1891 Mr. Blake had it correct. There was one very simple, clear, basic issue dealing with this debate, and that was the question of ultimate political union with the United States. That is what the issue and the real debate is all about. That is why the country is torn and divided, and so many Canadians feel anguished and anxious. They recognize that the step that has been initiated by the Government is the precursor to political union with the United States.
It has to do with the fundamentally different view of what Canada is and the vision we have, and whether we want to continue in the historical mission of Canadians, which is to carve out of the North American continent a northern region which has its own values, institutions, market-place, commerce, and its own way of doing things, or whether we want to allow, step-by-step, the integration of Canadians within their southern neighbour.
By the way, Mr. Blake's letter was instrumental in defeating the proposal in 1911. When the Minister for International Trade calls those who opposed the matter of 1911 "freaks of unreasoning panic", he was referring to members of the Conservative Party who opposed it at that time, as well as a large number of Liberals who also opposed it at that time. He forgets history very quickly.
In 1911 Canadian voters understood what the issue was all about. They understood that we were debating the independence of Canada. In 1946 the Liberal Government understood what the issue was about when it rejected that initiative. In 1972 when the same initiative was presented, the Trudeau Government understood what the issue of independence was about, because it also rejected it. In fact, a number of prominent Conservatives once understood what the issue was about.
In 1979 the then Leader of the Opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), stated on the question of free trade with the United States: "Free trade with the United States is like sleeping with an elephant". He could have used another euphemism: "When the lamb and the lion sleep together, the lamb does not get much sleep". That is the type of problem we face. He also stated: "Canadian plants would not be able to compete. Canadians rejected free trade with the United States in 1911, and they will do it again in 1983".
When presented with proposals on free trade put forward by his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) stated: "Presented as they are I find his proposals dangerous". The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated:

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Talk of bilateral free trade strikes me as simplistic and naive". I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and read the testimony of a whole range of prominent Conservatives who, at that point in time, were dead set against the whole notion.
There was one who was consistent, the Minister for International Trade. There is no doubt that the Member for St. John's West has been consistent right back to 1949 when he and his family fought against Newfoundland joining the Canadian union and fought instead for Newfoundland joining the United States. For 40 years he and his family have been consistent in attempting to have an integration, a union, with the country south of us. The Minister for International Trade is consistent to this very day. He understands the consequences. He knows what he is doing. When he rises, forget the blarney, knows what he is after. He is after the same thing that he was after in 1949, economic and political union with the United States. That is what the Minister for International Trade stood for then, and that is what he stands for now. I give him credit. At least he has been consistent, if stupid and wrong.
It is interesting, and one has to ask: "Why is it that all those prominent Conservatives, all the front bench of the present Government were so dead set in their opposition in 1979?" The conversion took place there. Somehow or other they changed their minds. Somehow or other they made that magic transformation to discovering that this trade arrangement was going to be the great bonanza of all times. One has to ask why. What is it that prompted that radical departure, that turn around, that denial of Canadian history, that denial of the objectives set by their own Leader, Sir John A. Macdonald, back in 1867 which have been supported by successive Canadian Governments of all stripes ever since? This is the first Government, the first Party, that has ever rejected that historical mission of Canada. What are the reasons?
A lot of mythology has grown up around this issue, fuelled by the propaganda machine; the $30 million that has been spent to create both fear and trembling in the Canadian public, and at the same time offering all kinds of candies on the tray. What is it that they are really saying? If one buys the mythology, which I do not, and I do not think anybody else will after this debate is over, the first thing is a promise of economic bonanza time. The Prime Minister and his Ministers are out there saying that there will be more jobs, more growth, more consumer spending. They create an image of people rushing down to Buffalo and buying cheap VCRs. All of a sudden there will be an incredible expansion and explosion of jobs in every region of the country.
The problem is that their own studies and reports completely deny those facts. When one looks at the economic growth figures, the economic benefits put forward by the Economic Council, by the Department of Finance, what do they say are the best optimistic assumptions? Let us look for a moment at the Department of Finance which is on the same side as the Minister for International Trade and the Prime Minister. After all, they are in the same Government. What do they promise? What does the Economic Council say will be the
maximum economic growth? They say 1/4 of 1 per cent per year. That is not even within the margin of error of the best computer forecaster. That type of margin could be wiped out by a change in the interest rate from week to week, or a change in the exchange rate from day to day. Yet, it is on that they are basing their great promise of cornucopia. Heaven will open for a 1/4 of 1 per cent. Not many Canadians will go out on to the streets and sing "Hallelujah" for a 1/4 of 1 per cent growth per year. Those are the Economic Council's figures.
I have read the Government's pamphlets on the consumer benefits. Those pamphlets are very skillful and sly. They never talk figures. I refer to the statements of Dr. Kerton, an economist for the Consumers' Association of Canada, who stated that the maximum saving, in other words, the best possible scenario that might accrue to consumers, is less than 1/5 of 1 per cent a year. That is a change that can take place in 24 hours in this country.
Pierre Racicot of the National Federation of Consumers' Association pointed out in front of the House of Commons standing committee that a household earning $20,000 might save $32 on this trade agreement over a 10-year period. Hallelujah! We have been saved. The great trade agreement, the great bonanza might save us $32 over a 10-year period, if we are lucky, and if it really works in the manner that they say it will.
At the same time what the Minister for International Trade did not talk about in all those economic promises is what the Conference Board talks about, and that is that it could increase the deficit by $2.5 billion. We saw the example in the last Budget. There was $500 million of additional taxation, one cent a litre on gasoline, to pay for the lost revenue in the first three-quarters of a year of the trade agreement. We either increase the deficit or raise taxes. There goes 1/5 of 1 per cent in consumer savings wiped out in a flash by the action of the Minister of Finance last February.
What the Government does not talk about are the job losses. Never is it mentioned that there will be industries affected. I was somewhat amused by the quotation used by the Minister for International Trade from Mr. Young, President of National Seafood, a good Maritimer. I have a letter here that was sent to me by Mr. Archie McLean, the Executive VicePresident of McCain's Foods, the largest Canadian food processor. He is a good Maritimer from New Brunswick. This letter was at the time when the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) was the Minister for International Trade. He wrote:
Dear Ms. Carney:
I am writing to you as a member of the Agricultural Sagit and as a hardcore Tory.
He is not a Grit, not a socialist but a hard-core Tory. He
says:
A comprehensive trade liberalization agreement between Canada and the U.S. which would remove tariff barriers and phase out non-tariff barriers
June 21, 1988

would devastate the dairy, poultry or feather, horticulture and beer and wine industries.
That is a hard-core Tory, head of the largest food processing firm in Canada, speaking. He says 70,000 jobs are at stake. Why? He says it is because the trade agreement neglects to take into account a couple of key points called weather and geography.
Mr. McLean points out in his letter that growing potatoes in New Brunswick or Manitoba costs $120 a tonne. They can be bought down south for $90 a tonne because there is a longer growing season there and less expense. He says he has a choice. He is either going to shut down or move south.
What does the Economic Council of Canada point out about jobs? It says that 186,000 jobs will be lost. Where will they be lost? They will be lost in key industries, electrical, machinery, manufacturing, printing and auto parts.
The Hon. Minister said that this would be a great salvation for the auto parts industry. Why is it then that Mr. Vic Lonmo, the President of the Auto Parts Manufacturers Association, appearing before our task force, said that 20,000 jobs are at risk as a result of this agreement? Who do we believe, the gentleman who heads this association or the Minister for International Trade a well-known extrovert?
The fact is that this Government has not been honest or straightforward in outlining these so-called economic benefits. It has hidden the real damage and the real costs and its own figures, studies and institutions totally deny the promises made. Time after time, the Prime Minister promises all these things. No wonder he can get away with it. The latest survey showed that 60 per cent of businessmen in Canada have not read the agreement yet. They are simply going on a wing and a prayer. They have not bothered to take the time to read the details of the agreement.
Canadian businessmen would not do that if they were signing a contract with a competitor or a client. They would hire the best lawyers. They would sit down and read the agreement fine point by fine point and decide if it was a good deal or not. In this case, they are going on theology, religion. They are going to take the word of honour, that sacred trust, of the Prime Minister for which he has become so well known. How can we disbelieve the Prime Minister who promised that he would not deindex senior citizens' pensions or that he would not enter into a free trade agreement?
When the Government begins to look at its own figures and those of the Economic Council, it will realize that that promise is not sufficient to even begin to warrant the kind of fundamental change that will be brought about in Canada. Those benefits are so meaningless as to be almost immeasurable.
What are we doing this for? We go to the second great ambition put forward by the Prime Minister. We remember that he said that we must gain secure access, a guarantee to
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
the U.S. market. In the House of Commons, the Right Hon. Prime Minister said that our highest priority is to have an agreement that ends the threat to Canadian industry and that a new regime on trade remedy laws must be part of the agreement. Is that what we got? Have we got a secure, guaranteed, fool-proof access for Canadian goods? It is an interesting case. Let us examine it.
First, let us examine the fear tactics the Government has used. It has tried to put forward the argument that, somehow, we have this evil presence to the south of us. It is kind of comical that government Members accuse Members of the Opposition of being anti-American, but they are the ones who have been going around the country saying: "Beware, the wolf is at the door. If we don't do something, those American Congressmen will violate us in our beds and therefore we need this deal in order to protect ourselves".
I went back and looked at the figures because I was kind of curious as to what in fact was going on. In the last 10 years, there have been some 40 trade remedy actions out of 600 taken by the Americans against Canada. Only eight of them came to a final decision and they included clothes-pins, nuts and bolts and optic sensing equipment. That has been the sum total of the American attack upon our economy, clothes-pins and nuts and bolts.
What the Government does not talk about is that in the same period of time, remedy measures have been available to us and we have taken six of those cases to GATT. We have won three of them. Two of them the Government plea-bargained outside the GATT process, and we know what happened on softwood lumber. That smart trick will cost the softwood lumber industry $800 million to $1 billion.
Over all, there has been a modest number of cases against us and we have succeeded in fighting off many of those cases. In the groundfish case of 1972, we were able to get a total withdrawal of the American legislation through a GATT ruling. The Americans have respected those rules and obligations.
Where is the fear coming from? It was primarily in the mind of the government spokesperson. In fact, there have been more initiatives by the United States Congress and the United States administration against Canada since 1984 than in the 10 years previous. Since the Tories came to power, there have been far more trade remedy actions against Canada than in double or triple the life of previous Governments.
After saying that, let us look at the insurance policy that we bought. The so-called dispute settlement mechanism applies U.S. law. We are still subject in every way, shape and form to the harassment techniques of U.S. industry when, if and how it wants to use it. Nothing has been gained. An American industry can still take an action before the International Trade Commission. It still has to go to the Commerce Department for a ruling. It still has to come back. It will still take one year to two years to get a decision. In the meantime, all those Canadian industries will still have to pay all their expenses and

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
deal with the harassment. Nothing has changed one iota except that what has changed is that if we go ahead with this agreement, we forgo our right to go to GATT which can provide a much quicker solution than the one put forward in the trade deal.
Under the present international rules, we can apply for an international panel after the first decision taken by the International Trade Commission. We will not have to wait for a year or two years. We can go right away and get a ruling.

speechtext:
Oh, here is a voice of wisdom. It takes five and a half months on average to get a panel decision. That is how much Hon. Members know. The stupidity and ignorance surrounding this deal bothers me. They simply do not know what they are talking about. They have not bothered to examine the alternatives. They have not bothered to examine the real facts. They simply buy the hocus-pocus. They are engaged in voodoo economics and therefore they believe in all the magic that goes with it.
The fact is that it takes an average of five and a half to six months to get an agreement. Therefore, I make the case that we will be worse off under the provisions of this agreement. It will take longer and cost more for Canadian business under this agreement than under the present arrangement.
What is the debate about? We did not get security of access. The Americans will still apply their laws and will slam-dunk us at every opportunity. In fact, they will be more encouraged to do so because they will have seen what a bunch of patsies we are. They know how much we have backed down, retreated and withdrawn every time the Americans get tough.
Naturally the Americans will use these instruments. In fact, the most important consequence of these negotiations is that in the implementing legislation the U.S. Congress is now considering, it has brought in a new trade measure directed against Canada, a measure which will give it the right to monitor all Canadian imports that may have a subsidy. If it does not like what it sees, the U.S. administration can take unilateral action and will not have to wait for an industry to do it.
The birth of the Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement has resulted in a new monster to attack us. That is the end result of this great negotiation by the Prime Minister and his Cohorts. We have an added problem that we did not have before.
Adding up the two levels of supposed benefits, the economic and the secure access, I think we have to admit that it is pretty questionable. If these "freaks of unreasoning panic" the Minister for International Trade spoke about had applied their rationality, they would have seen that it is a minor-league deal.
It just does not have much in it.
Remember when the Prime Minister was on television one night? He got his make-up on, his flags around him and a picture of the kids. He said: "Look, folks, you buy this deal,
we're going to have access to a $750-billion procurement market." What did we get? We got the difference between $170,000 and $25,000, about 1 per cent of that of which he promised. Not even close. That was a Class C effort, Mr. Speaker. He could not even make the majors on that. That is what is being sold across the country, as the great economic salvation for Canada.
They say, those are not the reasons why we have this trade deal or the Bill before us. That is not the reason why this Government has gone pall-mall into negotiations. The only way that we can fully determine the real reason is to look at the other side of the ledger, the cost side.
They do not talk about that. I have read their publications carefully. They do not tell you about the cost side. They do not tell you about the fundamental change that will take place in the policies dealing with foreign investment in this country. They try to pretend that somehow that is simply a small, trifling matter, that Mr. St. Laurent doesn't change anything, really.
I want to remind you of something, Mr. Speaker. Since the Tories came to power in 1984, there has not been one rejection of an application for foreign investment, not one. Not one has in any way troubled the minds of the monitoring process. Far more important, of the $22 billion of foreign investment that has come into this country since 1984, 94 per cent has been in takeovers and acquisitions, not new business, not creating new enterprise in Canada, but in takeovers and acquisitions of existing Canadian businesses.
This deal will entrench that kind of policy in an international agreement so that future governments cannot get at it. The whole agreement is based upon perpetuity. Doesn't that begin to tell you something? Doesn't that tell you that the real reason for the agreement has nothing to do with trade, but has an awful lot to do with trying to entrench, in perpetuity, a new kind of Conservative economic framework in this country, the market-driven framework, so nobody that else can get at it? That begins to tell you a little bit about what the real cost will be.
Let's look at other angles, energy and resources. That, as far as the Americans are concerned, is the centrepoint of the agreement. They will take everything else. What they have got is what they wanted for 40 years, total, free, complete, open access to Canadian resources untrammelled, unheeded, unrestrained, and unlimited. They got what they want.
This deal goes back to a proposition put forward by something called the Paley Commission in 1952 under President Eisenhower, when they said the number one priority strategically for the United States is to get full control over North American resources. Well, they got it. The Mulroney Government has given it to them right here. What does it mean? What it really means is this. In the crucial area of energy, it is perhaps the most valuable resource that we have
June 21, 1988

as a country in terms of our future economic development. What do we do? We freeze the price for ourselves. We can't use it to our advantage. We can't say that we will use the power of the public sector to create an advantage for Canadian industry in the use of our energy resources. That is prevented and prohibited in this agreement. We cannot have an export price for our mineral resources.
If we want to establish further programs to enhance value added of our natural resources, this agreement prohibits us from doing it. The whole idea of getting more jobs out of our natural resources is limited by this because the big resource corporations do not want it. They just want to ship that stuff as quickly and as fast as they can across the border.
What we are dealing with is the dismantling of a mixed economy. We are dealing with the evisceration of a political economy. We are dealing with an abandonment of the historic tradition of this country which is that we use a mixture of public and private initiative to build Canada.
The whole emphasis of this and why it gets support by the powerful forces and the economic corporations and the big players, is because they see this as a way of putting a strait-jacket around the federal and provincial governments of Canada. That is what they really want. That is the purpose behind the trade agreement. That's the sell-out of our independence. If we don't have that, we don't have our independence.
Once we deny and reject and withdraw the ability of Canadians through their democratically elected institutions to set public policy on economic and social questions, we no longer have a country worth a name.

speechtext: The Tories sold it out.
