speechtext:
If you don't believe me, go back to the agreement and read some of the other Articles. According to Clause 6, which gives the federal Government the override on any provincial jurisdiction, if any action, regulation, policy, piece of legislation, in a provincial legislature, does not accord with the terms of the agreement, the Government has an override. It can bring them to account bring them to heel. This brings a third partner to the whole federal-provincial relationship, the United States of America.
We now have the federal Government, the provinces and the Government of the United States negotiating our Constitution and negotiating our federal-provincial relations. When it comes to the issue of the division of powers or who has jurisdiction, it will not be a question of the balance between federal-provincial rights. The Americans will say: "We have a right here too. It is called the international trade agreement". We have a brand new Constitution being debated in this House at the very moment, bringing a brand new outside partner to the table.
As the upholder of the traditions of this House, Mr. Speaker, let me ask you this. Why, if you look at Clause 8 in the Bill, does Clause 8 say that the trade agreement supersedes
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
any Act of Parliament, any decision that we make? Now, the American Congress isn't quite so dumb. Their implementing legislation says the opposite. Their implementing legislation says that all Acts of Congress supersede the trade agreement. We are just now debating the giveaway of the sovereignty of this institution. Whether it is freedom of information or equity rights or any of the Bills we have passed, if they don't accord with this agreement, then forget it, they don't count.
When the Minister for International Trade tries to disparage the concerns raised by millions of Canadians about what this Bill will do, tries to laugh it off, tries to make a joke out of it, he is simply demonstrating a lamentable lack of understanding of his own legislation and what it means. He simply is trying to smokescreen, to cover up, the real purpose and intent of the Bill before us.
We have had debates in this House about the question of water. I want to deal with that for a moment. The Minister for International Trade and the Prime Minister, in all of their righteous indignation, have said there is absolutely no impact upon water in this agreement. Well, let me just go to the Bill. Let me go to the schedule of the Bill. Tariff item 22.01 states that it includes "waters, including natural waters". What does the interpretive note that is going out to all the custom officers across the Canadian borders say? This is the publication of the Government of Canada. The interpretive note on the new customs system says tariff item 22.01 covers ordinary natural water of all kinds.
The Hon. Minister has not dealt honestly with this House. That is the reading of his own document that he himself is responsible for. So, when he says it does not include water, there it is tariff 22.01 and the interpretive note that goes with it. It is quite telling that the question was asked of the Government: "Well, if you are so sure that water is not included, then you have a very easy recourse. Simply include an exemption in the Bill."
The American Congress has the right to include all kinds of new amendments but the Minister says we cannot do the same, we are not as good as they are. We asked the Minister to try one teeny one, an exemption for water. In response we got blank stares and silence. It was the only time in his life that the Minister for International Trade did not explode with a mounting pressure of fuminous gas.
He had no answer to that because they know full well that this agreement will give the Americans the right to demand the use of our water resources and that Canadians will no longer have the right to decide or choose otherwise because the agreement will be part of our Constitution, it will supersede every Act of Parliament. It will tell us what we can and cannot do in this country. That is the reality of it.
The Government says that social programs are not touched whatsoever. Well, the Bill clearly enunciates the principle of national treatment in the health management area. Taking

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
away the trade jargon terms it means that we cannot in any way provide a different set of rules or standards for Canadians than we provide for Americans. We have to treat them exactly the same. If an American management firm in health sciences, laboratories, or blood clinics want to set up a private operation, we cannot say no.
I predict that this area will become one of the major sources of combat in this country. As province after province begins to discover how their powers have been usurped to set credentials for their professionals and standards for their health care systems, they will rise up in revolt. I suspect that, like a lot of the business people, they have not yet read the agreement. They have not begun to understand the implications of it.
Aside from the specific question there is the much larger issue of harmonization. When the agreement comes into effect, if it does, and Canadian businesses find themselves dealing with competitors from the southern states where there are no right-to-work laws, no minimum wages, no taxes, and no social programs, they are going to ask how we expect them to compete with manufacturers who do not have to carry the same costs of health care.
The President of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, Mr. Thibeault said: "It's simply a fact that as we ask our industries to compete toe to toe with American industries, we in Canada are obviously forced to create the same conditions in Canada that exist in the United States, whether it's an unemployment insurance scheme, workmen's compensation, the cost of government, the level of taxation, or whatever".
I have page after page of similar quotes from Canadian businesses saying that when the deal is in place they will naturally have to ask the federal and provincial governments to change the rules on environment, workmen's compensation, and unemployment insurance.
For the Prime Minister and the Minister to say that there is no impact on social programs, that we will not see a change in the very carefully constructed, very important and creative network which we have built up in this country, is pure and simple conniving. That is the only word which can be prescribed. They are simply not telling it as it is. Their own business allies contradict them. The Americans contradict them. The whole thesis is that if they can only get this Bill by without telling the truth, if they can only keep the smoke machine running, maybe Canadians will not realize the implications of what they are doing.
In this debate my colleagues, in each of their roles, will be debating sector after sector, culture, energy, resources, social programs, and the environment, and pointing out how the deal encrusted in this legislation is a basic and fundamental restriction on the freedom and rights of Canadians to choose their own programs and policies.
It is not a matter of being for or against free trade. The fact is that there are other alternatives. We have put forward what we believe is a real and practical set of proposals on how to
bring down trade barriers without doing it at the price of our sovereignty and independence. We can do it in a way which will allow us to maintain an active, positive, and creative role in world affairs. We can build bridges to the Third World, design our own industrial strategies at home, and ensure that our relations with the United States and other trading partners are proper, creative, and expansive, all according to our own demand.
We are not arguing isolationism or continentalism, but for a form of internationalism. That is the real exciting, ambitious opportunity for Canadians who do not want to lock ourselves in fortress America. We do not want to start down the slippery road to further and further integration and further and further reduction of our powers, our rights, and our abilities to choose. Rather, we want to expand those opportunities. Canada has a rare opportunity in this day and age. We are seen by so many other countries as a potential leader of a coalition of other countries which will not engage in the game of power politics where "might makes right".
I reject the thesis which is coming out of the Summit that there is going to be an international triad of North America, Europe, and Japan which will run the world and the rest of the people can take the crumbs from the table. It is a thesis expressed by so many of the neo-Conservative leaders. That has not been the Canadian tradition. Dating back to World War II we have fought for internationalism, for small and large to be treated the same, for no discriminatory rules but a rule of law which treats everyone equally.
By this action we contribute to that North American fortress, to the idea of a triad, the idea that the big guys with muscles are going to determine and choose and all the rest of the countries can be dependent upon us. It is a new form of 19th century colonialism which is being talked about at the Summit, a kind of noblesse oblige, that we'll take care of the poor and disadvantaged.
I reject that, Mr. Speaker, and my Party rejects it. If we agree to this kind of deal we will be giving away the weapons we have. The fact of the matter is that there is another real option. We have said that we can get better security of access and better guarantees for our markets by strengthening and developing the international trade system, by using it in an effective way and being seen as strong supporters of that system rather than trying to scurry into the sanctuary of the continental market-place.
We have put forward proposals in that regard. We have put forward proposals on how to diversify our trade. The Minister for International Trade has said that this deal will lead to greater global opportunities. If that is the case, why is it that since 1984 when the Tories came to power our trade deficits with the Pacific Rim have gone from $700 million to $4.6 billion? Why has our trade with Latin America dropped close to 30 per cent and with Europe 20 per cent? Why is our trade surplus, which in 1984 was $17 billion, now down to $8 billion?
June 21, 1988

The reason is that our trade in every part of the world except the United States is going kaput. We are closing trade missions, stopping the funding for small businesses, and rejecting opportunities in the global market-place because we are so occupied and obsessed with the American market. That will be our future if this deal goes ahead. Canadian businesses will not expand, they will shrink and retreat. They will see the market in Akron, Ohio, and forget that there is one in Accra, Africa. That will be the problem.
We think we have to diversify our international marketplace. We can only achieve that if we begin, as a national entity, to invest in the very means to create a competitive international player. We must put money into training, research, and universities in order to build up human resources. That is the key to our international competitiveness.
Instead, in the last four years the Government has been cutting back on training programs, cutting back on aid to universities, and cutting back on research and development. The Government has been pulling back on the very investments which would make this country strong, able, and competitive.
There is a very clear alternative, Mr. Speaker. There is an option and a choice. It is not a matter, as the Government is trying to say, of being for or against opening trade markets. It is, rather, a question of how we are going to do it. Do we do it by burrowing ourselves into the continental fortress, or do we do it by expanding and opening our opportunities in a worldwide way?
As I pointed out, the reason why the Government rejects the much broader and more noble ambition is because that is not its agenda. Its agenda is to constrain the sovereign rights of future Canadian Governments. That is what is on the line with this legislation and that is what we will fight.
I say to my colleagues opposite that they are in for the fight of their lives, not in terms of procedural wrangling, but through a hard fought debate on the floor of this House and in the committee. Canadians will ultimately know the consequences of the Government's action and they will begin to understand what the debate is about. It is about the independence of this country. Whether we win or lose, we owe it to the future generations to make sure they understand what is happening here today. We are really fighting for the kind of Canada which we have known and believed in rather than for a pale, branch-plant imitation that has come forward under the leadership of the Prime Minister. That is the real debate before us. It is the most important debate to take place in this Chamber for generations to come.

Today's performance by the Minister for International Trade illustrates that he has completely lost sight of the importance of this legislation to the country. One can only say in the strongest possible terms that the Minister has not lived up to his responsibility to put before the House in a sensible manner the legislation we are debating today. Instead, we have seen an example of fear mongering, of blustering, of inaccuracy, irrelevancy and long-winded pomposity which has given us absolutely no insight whatsoever into this Bill.
It is a disgraceful performance. The Minister owes the House an apology for making that kind of speech at the beginning of such an importance debate.
This debate is one about choices. Canadians will have to decide which of three choices they want to make. First, do we follow this Accord with the United States and make ourselves essentially their resource periphery, dependent far more than we are now on their economy? If so, we accept the blustering pomposity of the Minister for International Trade as the prophet for the future of this country.
Second, do we follow essentially the same old path of the past with the Liberal ad hoc interventionism which consists of no strategy, no direction, no sense of leadership toward a new way to deal with our economy? It is an approach that hopes for the best and relies on GATT.
Third, do we accept that we finally try to build in this country an independent, fair economy and society using our rich resources? Do we try to develop an industrial game plan, a sense of direction which gives us a high tech future in the world? Do we look at full employment as a dominant objective over everything? Do we want to take the path that will make

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
us proud of ourselves in the world as a country that is independent and can stand on its own feet to operate successfully on an equal basis with every other country in the world?
I think that is the course we want to take. I believe that is the course that will be chosen when we finally get the election that is deserved on this issue. That is the course that this Party offers and that this Party has presented and will continue to stress to Canadians as this debate continues.
The Conservatives have lost faith in Canada. The great Liberal guru, Donald Macdonald, said: "Let's have a leap of faith". The Tories have gone one better and have had a leap of lost faith. Consequently, what we have is a branch plant manager, a branch plant Prime Minister, a branch-plant Party, and a branch plant policy that gives no sense of direction or future for this country and our children.
This Bill lets Canadians down, just as the past government let Canadians down with its gross patronage appointments. It is not just New Democrats with perhaps a partisan perspective, who see this deal this way. There was a statement from a group of completely non-partisan Canadians this week. They are people like Geogik Notsiof, one of our most senior former Ambassadors to the Soviet Union, a former Chancellor of the University of Toronto, Edgar Gallant, who is the former Chairman of the Public Service Commission, Eve Dubey, the former Dean of Social Sciences at Laval University, Louis Philip Blanchard, Director of the University of Moncton, G.W.F. McCain the head of McCain Foods, J.M. Kerion, the former Dean of Social Sciences at the University of Ottawa. They said very clearly, having looked at non-partisan observers who know something about politics and economics, who have no axe to grind, this statement of our concern is in no way motivated by anti-American considerations but rests only on our strong belief that the continuance of a distinct and prosperous Canada is important for Canadians and for the world as a whole.
They then went on to say that in their view, this accord with the United States, results in the following conclusion that our ability to survive as a distinct society in the world of tomorrow fades away and we could be caught in an irreversible process of complete absorption by our giant partner to the south.
That is not a statement that comes from partisans. It is a statement that comes from concerned Canadians who have looked at this deal and have seen not the great statistics about trade presented to us by the Minister for International Trade. They have seen the tremendous giveaways, the absurd sellouts, the disgusting surrender of our independence as a country which is shown at virtually every page in this accord with the United States.
The Minister did not talk about those things, but they are here and they will kill us as a country in the future as surely as our children follow us and their children will follow them.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that this does not come from a political party; it is a statement by individuals who have studied this Agreement, people like Yves Dube, former dean of the Faculty of Social Sciences at Laval University, Louis-Philippe Blanchard, rector of the University of Moncton, J.-M. Quirion, former dean of Social Sciences at the University of Ottawa, who concluded after much study that the price of this Agreement for Canada is high and the risks for our future as a distinct society very great. So our ability to survive as a distinct society is in danger of declining rapidly and we would be caught in an irreversible process of integration with our giant partner.

That is the reality which exists and that is the reality which has to be seen by Canadians in the election that will come. They have to see that reality, but they also have to see the tremendous anti-democratic process by which the Conservatives have tried to jam this Bill through the Parliament of Canada. The Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade had but 10 days to go across the country to allow the people of Canada to comment, not on the agreement itself but on this mere summary which had been released. Would the committee with its massive Tory majority even look at the actual agreement? Would it look at the differences between it and the summary? Not a chance. It would keep to
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   TRADE EXPORT OF WATER
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   TRADE EXPORT OF WATER
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should enact legislation to prohibit the large-scale export of water from Canada to another country.
He said: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am happy to be able to rise and present this motion today, calling upon the Government to bring forth legislation that would prevent the large scale exports of water from our country to another.
The reason for the motion, Mr. Speaker, is that today there is no legislative mechanism available to the people of Canada to prevent a Government, whether it is this Government or the
COMMONS DEBATES___________________June 21, 1988
Export of Water
one that replaces this Government, or another Government years from now, from arbitrarily allowing the large scale export of water. I liken it to a municipal and a provincial law, which is a zoning by-law, which establshes the rules but provides for the ability to change that in a public forum.
If this Government would live up to its policy statements- and I will come back to those in a moment-and enact legislation, it would be like a zoning by-law that would force the Government of the day, if it decided that for whatever reason the export of water was appropriate, to come back to this House to receive the approval of the duly elected representatives of the people of Canada.
There is no doubt that water is increasingly being recognized by Canadians as not just another resource, but as a common property of immeasurable value. It is increasingly becoming the focus of our attention, in terms of Government policy, and I suggest it will and should continue to do so.
Front and centre in this debate is the issue of water exports and inter-basin transfers. While this is only one aspect of the immensely complex problems facing us, in terms of water policy, it is an aspect which synthesizes the approach and the commitment to protecting our water resources.
I want to begin my comments today, Mr. Speaker, by commending both the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), and the Liberal environment critic. The recently released federal water policy states, definitively: "The Government of Canada emphatically opposes large-scale exports of our water". For this, the Minister should be commended.
As Well, the Liberal critic, the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), introduced a private Members' Bill a couple of years ago which called for a ban on water exports. While we had some problems with some of the aspects of the Bill, the sentiment was very appropriate, and I commend him for that.
I want, to read into the record some comments made by people who have examined this issue, have researched it, and have offered their thoughts for public consumption. The first is from the American Review of Canadian Studies, 1986. It is a paper called: Canadian Water Exports, A Controversy in the Making written by Geoffrey R. Weller, the Vice-President of academics at Lakehead University, in the community of Thunder Bay. He writes:
The Canadian economy has long been heavily dependent upon the export of natural resources ranging from fur, lumber and grain to minerals of all kinds. Up until now water has been regarded differently and not exported in any large amounts. However, Canada is entering an era in which there is mounting pressure to change the generally held view of water as being beyond market forces and not available for export.
Canada is regarded by some as having abundant supplies while other nations have increasing shortages and Canada is seen as being, therefore, in a position to gain significantly from the export of a valuable commodity, much as if it were what might be called "blue gold".
Perhaps the most notable exponent of the benefits of exporting Canada's water resources both directly and indirectly in the form of hydro-electric power is the current premier of Quebec, Mr. Robert Bourassa. Not only is he
identified with the massive James Bay project but recently, with the publication of his book Power from the North and his becoming premier, he has been associated with a desire for further large-scale hydro developments in northern Quebec and the Kierans Grand Canal scheme.
The latter involves making James Bay into a freshwater lake, diverting the water from there to the Great Lakes and from there to arid regions in the United States and Canada.
There has been concern in Canada about the issue of water exports before but it has never been as great as it is at the present. Some large-scale schemes were proposed in the mid nineteen-sixties that caused public concern.
I remember well the committee called Damn the Dams, which formed in northwestern Ontario, to prevent the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers from proceeding to survey our watersheds, with a mind to developing a system to divert water through Lake Superior into the United States. Mr. Weller continues:
In addition, books have occasionally appeared on the subject in the past two decades, most notably D. Booking's Canada's Water for Sale?, in 1972, and Foster and Sewell's The Emerging Water Crisis in Canada in 1981, and these have kept some awareness of the issue alive. Water export never, however, really reached the forefront of the agenda of industry, environmental and other pressure groups, or government. This was partly because the schemes devised seemed so grandiose and fanciful, even in the era of mega-projects; partly because the need for water in dry areas was not seen as an urgent or immediate one (especially in Canada); and partly because water was regarded as a public good that was and should be free of market forces.
Many Canadians, hearing more and more of the degradation and usage patterns of water in both Canada and the United States, are becoming increasingly aware that water is not a limitless resource. It does possess considerable value, and may therefore be eyed covetously by those who are short of it and by those who can make money by exporting it.
A further reason water exports are being taken seriously is that the new orthodoxy in economics is no longer sympathetic to an object such as water being a public good, and free of market forces. Consequently, it is entirely possible that if it were to be viewed as a consumption good, like any other, it could well be available for export, under the right terms and conditions.
One of the elected representatives in the United States thinks that way. Jim Wright, who is now the Speaker of the United States Congress, wrote in 1966:
There is to the north of us a stupendous supply of water, enough to satisfy our predictable wants for years to come, which is simply going to waste. We need the water. We need to develop the means of getting that water.
There are politicians south of the border who are looking northward. I would suspect, because of the increasing drought situations in the United States, as well as in Canada, that there, too, will be people who will be eyeing us, with envy, wanting to get our water.
An acquaintance of mine, a Professor at the University of Minnesota, in Duluth, UMD, is working in co-operation with Lakehead University, developing Nordic studies and developing Great Lakes basin studies. Douglas Nord, who is one of the professors there, heading the Political Study Section, wrote a paper entitled Managing a Regional Resource, the Case of the Great Lakes. In the section entitled "Marketing a Regional
June 21, 1988

Resource-Exporting Water From the Great Lakes", he writes:
In speaking before a 1982 Great Lakes Water Conference former Wisconsin Governor Lee Sherman Dreyfus, observed:
Over two hundred years ago Ben Franklin said, 'We know not what the well is worth until it runs dry'. We in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Ontario, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Quebec, New York must now look to our well.
God and the glacier created the Great Lakes but Ottawa and Washington, D.C., will try to claim it. If we don't stand together now and protect and preserve that which by historical chance belongs to the people within whose state and provincial borders these lakes exist, then I say we will be letting loose the greatest resource ever given to any people on this continent.
He further quotes a Canadian, Ralph Pentland of the Inland Water Directorate of Environment Canada who feared that:
"Once the tap is turned on, you can't turn it off. If you start a diversion of water, you build up a whole economic infrastructure dependent upon that source of water... At that point, you can't stop. You've sold your sovereignty, your heritage and your future.
That is why I bring forth this motion today. I want the Government of Canada to come forth with legislation which will very clearly indicate in law-not in policy but in law- that our water is not for sale, that our water is not going to be massively shifted from Canada to another country. The country which would most logically come to mind would be the United States, although there is the potential for large scale shipments by seagoing vessels to move water elsewhere. I am concerned that while the Government may make all the right sounds in its heart it is not prepared to go the next step.
I would like to refer to comments made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was interviewed by Fortune magazine a couple of years ago. He indicated that Canada would consider water exports to the U.S. if such an idea were mutually beneficial and economically feasible. "Why not?", he was quoted as saying. That is the kind of response which makes me worried.
It is not only the Prime Minister. It is well known, also, that Canada's negotiator for the trade deal, Mr. Simon Reisman, is an avid supporter of the Grand Canal scheme. He told an Ontario Economic Council seminar a couple of years ago that linking water exports to trade would be a brilliant way of getting the U.S. enthusiastic about the trade deal. Did he carry out this brilliant idea? Well, the Government has steadfastly denied that there is any connection. It has repeated often that there is nothing in the trade deal which forces us to sell water to the United States.
You may have noticed that that is an interesting way of putting the case for the protection of our water. In fact, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) took the wind out of his own argument when he went on to say that there is nothing in the trade deal which forces us to sell anything to anyone.
Export of Water
The Government had the option of insisting that there be an exemption in the trade deal which would specifically exempt water exports. It has been suggested by senior government officials that the Government had, in fact, wanted a water exemption but that it caved in at the eleventh hour. Why? We can only assume that it was in order to get the U.S. to agree to a deal.
The Minister for International Trade can bluster all he wants, but as long as the trade deal simply looks at water as another resource, the same as all the others, it remains open to exploitation as a marketable commodity.
That is why I have put forward this motion. I am not asking for a lot. I am simply asking the government Members and the Official Opposition to give their support to this legislation so that we can protect our water and entrench that will in legislation.
There is a sense of urgency about this motion. Even if we were to begin today, with the best of efforts, to enact policy to protect our water, we would still be facing many years of continued pollution and overuse of a dwindling supply of accessible fresh water. Despite many years of warnings by environmentalists and scientists, as a nation we have been very slow to come to terms with the deplorable state of our water supplies. We have not grasped the urgency that this problem demands.
Perhaps this is due, in large part, to an understandable misconception about our water supplies. When you stand on the shore of Lake Superior outside my home in Thunder Bay and look out toward the horizon it is very difficult to believe that Canada is not a water rich country. However, that is exactly the case.
The Government's federal water policy sets out a compelling case in this regard. It points out that Canada, which occupies about 7 per cent of the world's land mass, has 9 per cent of renewable water, just about a fair share. However, about 60 per cent of that fresh water drains northward, away from our population, and is inaccessible. That which is accessible is mostly polluted.
There has always been a feeling that the need to get serious about protecting our water supplies was a problem for the future. Well, Mr. Speaker, the future is here. We cannot afford to put off any longer addressing this issue which quite literally is a matter of life and death.
I submit that the place to start is with a ban on exports. I say this for a variety of reasons. To begin with, water comes predominantly under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Any legislation, any progressive moves toward cleaning up and protecting our water supplies, must be subject to negotiations with provincial governments. However, water exports come under the purview of the federal Government. While I believe it is still beneficial to consult with the provinces on this matter, it is an area in which the federal Government can move

June 21, 1988
Export of Water
quickly, demonstrating leadership and setting the groundwork for the approach that must be taken.
Let me add to the argument the words of Robert Fournier, the Chairman of the Water Resources Committee. He says:
Water is a vital element in Canada's past; it is equally vital for its future. Where once water determined the pattern of exploration and settlement, it now enhances the beauty and character of the landscape and plays a powerful role in Canadian identity. For all these reasons, and in the sheer abundance of our waters, Canadians can and do take pride.
Thus it is cause for particular concern that the impact of current trends and future events on Canada's waters is uncertain. Climatic change, rise in sea levels, increasing abuse, and a potential export demand all place the future availability of water in doubt. This highlights the fact that Canadians are not owners of water, but hold only limited stewardship rights. Water returns to us both the benefits and disasters of our civilization. Technology can and does impact on our waters in more than one direction. Given the importance of water, the development and application of science and technology to assure wise management is vital to meet national needs.
The Minister, in his response to the federal water policy said:
That is why the Government of Canada emphatically opposes large-scale exports of our water. We have another reason for our opposition; The interbasin diversions necessary for such exports would inflict enormous harm on both the environment and society, especially in the North, where the ecology is delicate and where the effects on Native culture would be devastating.
I think it makes an awful lot of sense for us to support this motion in order to send a message to the Government that this House desires legislation which will control, prevent or restrict-whatever terms we want to use-the export of water from Canada to another country. I urge all Members of this House to give it their support and allow it to come to a vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have been around this House a long time and you know how the water issue stirs the emotions of all people including parliamentarians, and there is no exception today. The Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) has certainly done us a service by bringing forward his motion which is very simple and straightforward. It asks the Government to enact legislation to prohibit the large scale export of water from Canada. It could not be clearer than that. The message has been elaborated upon by the Member. I wish to thank him for his kind words and to express my support.
The timing of this motion, I hope you will agree, Mr. Speaker, is particularly appropriate because we are debating today the trade deal between Canada and the U.S.A. For that reason alone the issue of water becomes charged with emotion because there are in that trade deal certain commodities spelled out for exclusion from it but we do not see water among them.
I refer to the fact that there is in the trade deal a specific reference for exclusion from the application of what the trade deal would be all about to beer, lumber, and unprocessed fish.
Evidently one wonders if it was desirable for the Government of Canada to identify these three items. The chief
negotiator for Canada has a record of making public statements in favour of major water diversions. Two years ago, the National Research Council made a grant of some $30,000 available to the Grand Canal Company, which now and then raises its head to propose a diversion scheme of monstrous dimensions and implications. Considering all of these precedents, it is no wonder that the question of water export becomes increasingly acute in parliamentary and political terms. Therefore, there is a convergence of legislative proposals that we are required to address here today.
Why should there be legislation? It is very simple: One does not want governments of the future to perhaps approve a measure of water diversion or export on a large scale without parliamentary approval. Presently, this is possible because there is no legislation to give Parliament these powers. We must deal with that vacuum. That is why the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan is moving his motion and it is for the very same reason that two years ago in February, 1986, we debated my Bill C-257 which had the same intention.
This matter is still unresolved, despite the fact that the Government has had an opportunity to examine and reply to the Pearse water report that was published in 1986. It has not taken the necessary legislative initiative to give a future Parliament the opportunity to intervene with the help of legislation and discuss any proposal of this nature emanating from the executive, as we are doing today with the trade deal. That opportunity is denied parliamentarians unless they have the required legislation.
The importance of keeping waters within the boundaries of Canada has already been stressed. Let me repeat for the record what was said in 1947 by then Minister St. Laurent about water export policy: "Can we in fairness to Canadian generations of the future allow such natural wealth to be diverted from our own territory and put to uses from which it would be extremely difficult afterwards to withdraw it?" That well expressed thought today finds a modern meaning in terms of dependence. Once we create a dependence for water in other national jurisdictions it becomes virtually impossible to turn the tap off.
The Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan has already referred to General McNaughton's statement to this effect. Not only does the importance of water have an impact on the Canadian psyche, it is significant to the national identity of this country, particularly with respect to its economic uses.
Obviously, at the point we would become involved in large scale diversion and export of that water, we would also be exporting a considerable amount of jobs and economic interests. That is not in the short-term or long-term interests of Canada.
Evidently, the water that would be exported in a large-scale export would come from areas on which native people depend for their lifestyle. It would have a disruptive effect and would create an even greater dependence on non-aboriginal society. It would cause significant cultural dislocation. Therefore, it is no
June 21, 1988

wonder that native people have frequently expressed their natural and understandable opposition to water diversion. To them, water is part of their lifestyle and not just another commodity.
In conclusion, let me summarize the points that have been made in advancing this motion and other Bills during the life of this Parliament. It signals to the Government that it must come to grips with the necessity of putting forward enacting legislation on this very important subject.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add a few comments to the motion which has been proposed that, in the opinion of this House, the Government should enact legislation to prohibit the large scale export of water from Canada to another country.
Let me explain the evolution of the federal policy on water since we formed the Government in 1984. In 1985, a year after we became the Government, the priorities and planning committee of Cabinet empowered the Minister of the Environment to act for the Government in formulating a federal water policy. He gave that matter a very high priority. Cabinet further decided that until this policy was in place there would be no major interbasin diversions or large scale exports of water.
The first step in developing the water policy was an inquiry on federal water policy headed by Dr. Peter Pearse of the University of British Columbia, which reported to the Minister of the Environment in September, 1985. Its mandate was to consider the nature of emerging issues, the state of the resource, future requirements for water, interjurisdictional dimensions and scientific and research expertise, with a view to ensuring enhancement of the health, well-being and prosperity of the people of Canada.
In conducting its work, the inquiry actively sought the views of provincial, territorial and federal Government Departments and their agencies, of private citizens and public groups, of industry and of the academic community. Between late September and early December of 1984, 201 presentations were heard in 33 days of hearings in 17 locations across Canada. Over 300 written submissions were received. In addition, the inquiry commissioned 22 research papers on special problems related to this topic. The inquiry made 55 recommendations in its final report entitled Currents of Change. Three of those dealt with water export. The inquiry concluded: "It would be imprudent for the federal Government to reject all exports out of hand". It went on to say that the Government " ... should clearly set out the conditions that must be met for any proposal to be acceptable", and that there should be "clear procedures for assessing export proposals".
Those are three specific points made with respect to the export of water should Canada consider it. The inquiry simply said it would be imprudent for the federal Government to reject all exports out of hand, that we must clearly look at all
Export of Water
of the factors that would be involved and all the procedures necessary.
In November, 1987, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) released Canada's first comprehensive federal water policy statement. I would like to quote some of the comments made by the Minister at that time. He stated:
The truth is that Canada, which occupies 7 per cent of the world's land mass, has 9 per cent of its renewable water. Further, about 60 per cent of Canada's fresh water drains north, while 90 per cent of our population lives within 300 kilometres of our southern border. In other words, to the extent that we Canadians have lots of water, most of it is not where it is needed, in the populated areas of the country. In those populated areas where it is plentiful, water is fast becoming polluted and unusable. The over-all problem in the country is compounded by drought in certain regions. Put simply, Canada is not necessarily a water rich country.
The Minister went on to say:
That is why the Government of Canada emphatically opposes large scale exports of our water. We have another reason for our opposition; the interbasin diversions necessary for such exports could inflict enormous harm on both the environment and society, especially in the North, where the ecology is delicate and where the effects on native cultures could be very harmful.
The Minister further stated:
The Government of Canada has the constitutional authority to block large scale export proposals. We can exercise this authority through various pieces of existing legislation. These include the Fisheries Act, The Navigable Waters Protection Act, the International River Improvements Act, and the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act.
And, as the policy makes clear, the federal Government is reviewing existing laws, administered by various federal agencies, with a view to strengthening federal legislation, to the extent necessary, to fully implement the water policy. When this review is complete and if further legislation is needed to give effect to the federal policy against large scale exports of water, then that legislation will be placed before Parliament.
From these excerpts from the Minister's speech I think we can see that he has expressed some very serious concerns. Although we appear to have lots of water, it is in our far North and it drains towards the North, but it is in the South that we need it. Further, he is saying there is a very serious concern about the diversion of our water with respect to environmental factors, ecological effects and the impact that large scale diversion of water would have on our native population, particularly in the North.
The Minister went on to say that we have within our jurisdiction the ability to deal with this question and that when that review is complete, any further legislation that is necessary would be brought before the House. So I think the position of the Government is very clear. We are concerned with protecting our water and the impact diversion could have if we were to enter into any large scale export.
I would also like to make a few comments to the Member who introduced the motion. He talked about the timeliness of his motion, in his mind. I think he was relating the sense of his motion to the debate we are having on the free trade agreement. Much has been said in the House of late about the impact of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement on the export of Canada's supply of fresh water, and misleading statements have been made. I think it is important to say that

June 21, 1988
Export of Water
the free trade agreement explicitly recognizes that the Governments of both countries have the right to protect their environment and conserve their natural resources. Nothing in the free trade agreement affects the federal water policy announced by the Minister last November. That policy clearly states that the Government will not permit the large scale export of water or the diversion of Canada's rivers to the United States.
I find it interesting that just because something is not explicitly excluded in the free trade agreement, somehow it is implicitly included. With that kind of logic, the sun, the moon and the stars are included. With that logic, the Liberal Opposition is included. With that logic the NDP is included. I cannot understand why these people constantly get up in the House and tell us that we have to exclude it. It is not in there. They are trying to make people believe, through their fear and propaganda and so on, that somehow it is mysteriously there. My goodness, the air is not excluded so I guess we had better add that too. Some of the hot air those Members produce over there should definitely be included.
We have to come to grips with what is fact and what is not fact. We have to start to recognize what is clearly there. Water is not in the free trade agreement other than bottled water, and the tariffs on that will come off. We have every right and every power under the free trade agreement to preserve our natural resources, and we shall do so.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am pleased to see the interest in Canada's water resources shown by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus). The Government and indeed the vast majority of Canadians share his concern over large water export projects. Let me deal with these concerns for a few moments.
Canada is without doubt one of the most favored nations in the world for its abundant fresh water resources. However, despite what most observers think, these resources are far from inexhaustible or indestructible. The situation of our underground waters is not as well understood as that of some other countries, mainly because we have relied a great deal on our surface waters. Canada probably has more lake area than any other country in the world. Our lakes play a major role in regulating the flow of our waterways seaward, and they provide a rich habitat for our fauna and flora and for our own enjoyment. However, most Canadian lakes are a one-time gift we were left after the last ice age. They are not renewable, except at the expense of the streams and rivers that feed and drain them.
Hence, the best way to measure a country's water reserve is to measure the renewable water supply from spring water and ground water. If we consider the average annual flow, Canadian streams and rivers represent nearly 9 per cent of the world's renewable water supply, or roughly 100,000 cubic metres per second. Considering the population of Canada which is only 1 per cent of the world's population, this supply is indeed a generous gift of nature, but these figures are not so out of proportion if we compare them with Canada's surface area which corresponds to approximately 7 per cent of the world's territory. In any case, these figures are well below the 25 to 40 per cent of the world's water supply often attributed to Canada in new reports that neglect to make a distinction between renewable and non-renewable sources.
For the sake of comparison, the total run-off from American streams and rivers, including Alaska, is estimated at approximately 94,000 cubic metres per second, or nearly 8 per cent of the world's supply, while the renewable supply of the USSR is 139,000 cubic metres per second, or nearly 13 per cent.
Despite the apparent abundance of water in Canada, there are other factors that shape our perception of these water resources. For instance, about 36 per cent of annual precipitation in Canada falls in the form of snow, most of which stays as such for several months until spring thaw. There are times when the run-off is many times greater than average, sometimes causing flooding, while there are also times when it only amounts to a fraction of the average figure. The geographic distribution of water is another problem, in that nearly two-thirds of the total run-off flows North, far from the more populated regions in the South.
June 21, 1988

The variations in precipitation from month to month and from year to year also affect the availability of water, and this summer is a case in point. These variations force us to consider not only the average flow but also the less reliable flow on which we can count only nine years out of ten.
The message we get from all this is that the total flow of Canadian rivers and streams does not constitute a realistic estimate of the water supply available to Canadians. Today, however, we do, on the whole, have annual reserves that are greater than our draw-off at the national level.
Thermal generating stations and the manufacturing industry are responsible for the greatest draw-off. As for irrigation, not the quantity of water drawn off but the quantity consumed is important, and the fact that irrigation is concentrated in the arid Prairies. In this region, Mr. Speaker, irrigation represents 87 per cent of all water consumption. The use by the manufacturing and mining industries and by towns and cities is another major source of draw-off. This, however, is not the sum total of water use.
It is difficult and sometimes impossible to calculate accurately local water use so as to ensure the survival of fish and fauna, protect our heritage, and provide for recreation, navigation, and the dilution of effluents.
Like the rest of the world, we Canadians are barely beginning to realize just how much water we will need to maintain the natural habitat, especially in light of efforts made by environment defence organizations, reports such as Global 2000 and the World Environment Commission.
Mr. Speaker, we do not usually consider water in a continental context but I believe it would be appropriate to compare our situation with that of the Americans. However I am making this comparison after seriously reflecting upon the situation of water quality which might further reduce the supply of water that is acceptable and can serve for various uses. As I said earlier, we must also keep in mind the fact that we did not figure out local water needs.
An examination of the balance between reserves and consumption reveals that some Canadian regions already experience water shortages despite the fact that the world's renewable reserves exceed current consumption. The main region facing such problems is the southern part of the Prairies, particularly the north and south basins of the Saskatchewan River, the Red River, the Assiniboine River and the Milk River where they are considering proposed water supply storage facilities and small projects to transfer water between basins.
With respect to demand, water consumption trends closely parallel our two countries' demographgic densities and different needs. To meet the water consumption requirements of people, municipalities or thermal energy producing companies as well as those of the industrial and agricultural sectors, the United States now take from surface and underground
Export of Water
reserves quantities of water which are about 12 times larger than those we use in Canada, yet they outnumber us 9 to 1.
Right now, thermal energy production and manufacturing activities in Canada account for most of the consumption. Irrigation projects rank first in the United States and if that trend should continue for a number of years it might lead to disputes between those who favour energy production and others who are more supportive of local consumption in the southwestern United States where most of the irrigation facilities are located.
Without Alaska, water reserves in the continental United States are 60 per cent of Canada's. If we consider reserves that are reliable nine years out of ten, the flow in the United States is declining even more and represents slightly more than twice the draw-off. At the regional level, the ratio is in many cases even less promising.
According to a national assessment carried out in 1978, the Americans predicted there would be serious water supply problems between now and the year 2000 in seventeen subregions, which means in most of the Great Plains and the Southwest. This explains the sustained interest shown by certain "unofficial" circles in Canadian water "surpluses" that would enhance the demography and economy of these regions.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding I may add that major water exports, including diversions from one basin to another, were discussed in the Federal Water Policy published by the Minister of the Environment last November. I would like to quote briefly from what the Minister said in his introduction to this policy, and I quote: "To put it bluntly, Canada is not a country with an adequate water supply. That is why the Canadian Government is firmly opposed to large-scale exports of water. There is another reason, however. The diversions between basins that such exports would require would be extremely harmful, both to the environment and to society, especially in the North, where the natural environment is fragile and such projects would have disastrous consequences for our native cultures".
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's motion is generally in line with the present Government's policy on water exports. However, we already have substantial legislative power that we could use in this respect, and I am about to finish Mr. Speaker. We are now looking at the situation to determine whether we should reinforce those powers, and if that is the case, I can assure you that the present Government will take any action necessary to preserve our invaluable water resources.

He is proposing to dam the Souris River, and two dams and reservoirs are proposed: The Alameda being one, and the Rafferty being another.
The Souris River depends entirely upon run-off. If that dam had been built in 1912, the first year they started to measure the flow of the Souris River, those reservoirs would not have been full until 1948. That is how much water is in the Souris River. Various studies have shown that, if Mr. Devine's reservoirs are to fill up, he will need water from some other sources. Of course, the nearest source is thousands of acres of wetlands. He is going to drain that, with tremendous impact on the environment in that area, but that will not be enough, especially in dry years. The Government of Saskatchewan's own study shows that there is a 20 per cent chance of not having a sufficient amount of water in the reservoir.
One cannot go ahead with a project of over $1 billion with that high a percentage of chance that there will not be enough water. Of course, they are now actively studying taking water from the Qu'Appelle River and the Qu'Appelle Basin in the heart of my riding. There is not enough water in the Qu'Appelle River and the Qu'Appelle Basin. I could take you there, Mr. Speaker, and show you that the level of the water in the river and in those lakes has dropped.
If the plumbing is in and the Qu'Appelle Basin is going to be connected to the Souris, when it comes time to determine if water is going to be taken out of the Qu'Appelle Basin, and there is over $1 billion invested in a power project, one knows darn well they will be taking water out of the Qu'Appelle rivers and lakes.
There are studies undertaken by the federal Government and the provincial Government that will also divert water from the South Saskatchewan River Basin via Diefenbaker Lake into the Qu'Appelle chain down into the Souris River.
While the Government talks about being opposed to the inter-basin transfer of water, it is actually involved in studying that in order to allow Mr. Devine his political rewards by building a power project and the accompanying dams that have no economic justification, that are environmentally damaging, and the only reason is pure and simple pork-barrel politics. The Government and the Minister of the Environment have knuckled under to the political blackmail committed by the thugs in the provincial Government in Saskatchewan, and it is disgraceful. For government Members to rise in the House and assure us how virtuous the Government is in terms of water policy 1 call hypocritical.
The other aspect that is most disturbing is that when water is diverted and the connections are done between the Souris River, the Qu'Appelle River, and the South Saskatchewan River, the plumbing will be in place to divert water to the United States. By treaty we are committed to sending 50 per cent of the historic level of what flows through the Souris down into North Dakota. That means that in a dry year like this year North Dakota will be assured of a steady supply of water. No wonder the Americans are going to give $40 million to the Saskatchewan Government to help with that dam project.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour to take part in this historic debate. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) have made clear, this is much more than a debate about establishing a stronger, more secure trading relationship with the United States. This debate in fact is about building a stronger and more secure Canada, a Canada that is better able to meet the needs and fulfil the hopes of people in every part of the country in the 1990s and in the new century beyond.
I take particular pride in speaking in support of this legislation. It was three and a half years ago that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought forward on behalf of the Government a comprehensive agenda for renewal of the Canadian economy. At the heart of that agenda was the belief that Canadians must and would rise to the challenge of the increasingly competitive international environment in which we make our living.
This challenge was met by the Government, and we embarked on a wide-ranging series of actions to create a better economic framework for risk taking, for innovation and for hard work. Of course, this is what has always made the difference between economic success and failure, but we need a framework for that to happen, a framework in which Canadians have both the scope and the incentive to seize economic opportunities, to give their best to the creation of new growth, jobs and a higher standard of living.

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement [Translation]
That is why we acted to restore fiscal responsibility to the federal government; to reduce, through deregulation and privatization, the burden of government intervention; to foster a healthy and receptive climate for private sector investment; to make regional development more sensitive to local needs; and to establish a more effective policy for the promotion of science, technology and innovation.
To further improve the framework for growth and job creation, Mr. Speaker, we embarked on comprehensive tax reform to make the tax sustem fairer for individual Canadians and more effective in supporting productive economic activity.
The Bill we are debating today is another crucial plank in our program for economic renewal that will ensure Canadians the greatest possible scope for their economic efforts. The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement will open up Major new opportunities for Canadians to benefit from expanded and more secure access to the richest market in the world.
The key word, Mr. Speaker, is benefit.
I want to outline the economic benefits that this bill opens up for Canadians in every part of the country.

The extent of these benefits is large. One of the most important benefits of the free trade agreement is lower prices and more choice for Canadian consumers. Our Department of Finance study estimated that the effect of the agreement will be to reduce over-all consumer prices in Canada by about 1 per cent by 1993, and these lower prices will in turn boost real personal disposal income and increase consumer spending.
As a result of lower prices and increasing wages, we are projecting a 2 per cent increase in consumer spending by 1993 over and above what would otherwise occur. Once all bilateral tariffs have been fully eliminated, the cost of consumer goods imported from the United States will be reduced by about 5 per cent on average. Business will gain from these lower prices and intermediate goods imported from the U.S that go into their production will also gain. Consumers in turn will benefit from lower prices on these goods. We hear a great deal about the other parts of the free trade agreement. Let us not forget that it means lower prices for consumers right across Canada.
As Canadian firms restructure and retool their factories to take advantage of new opportunities which will be brought to them through free trade, because we will secure strong access to the American market, business investment in plant and equipment is projected to rise by more than 4 per cent in real terms by 1993. Of course, that means economic activity, greater wealth and increased opportunities for employment.
The favourable impact of free trade on real personal incomes as well as on profits and consumer spending will translate into faster growth and job creation. As the Minister of State for Finance, that is a part of my responsibility, and free trade is part of promoting that. We estimate that 120,000
net new jobs will be created by 1993, the fifth year of the implementation of the agreement.
Just as important as the creation of new jobs is the fact that the thousands of existing jobs will be protected as a result of this agreement. These are jobs that would otherwise be jeopardized by increases in U.S. protectionism. This is too often forgotten. Not only will more jobs be created, but one of the greatest reasons for locking in a trading arrangement like this with the United States is to lock in access to the American market, and that will protect Canadian jobs.
In fact, the figures on job creation understate the over-all gains to be made. They are conservative in comparison to other reported estimates. There are many unquantifiable benefits as well that will further enhance the job gains to be made as Canadians take advantage of new economic opportunities that will be created.
Thinking of my own city, General Motors Diesel, for example, will be closing its locomotive plant in Illinois and expanding production in London. It could not do this if it were not able to move those locomotives back across the border into the United States with no tariffs and with less secure access. Another example is 3M which is also located in London. It has some facilities in Iowa that it is thinking of closing down and moving to Perth and London because they are closer to the over-all heart of the North American market.
Southwestern Ontario is one-day's truck drive from 62 per cent of U.S. payroll. We are beautifully situated in Canada to take advantage of new opportunities in the American market. We cannot quantify all of these opportunities, but they are there over and above the basic projections of the Department of Finance, and they also will, I think, increase further because of reduced production costs due to the rationalization that will occur. As a matter of fact, the third volume of the Macdonald Royal Commission points out that rationalization has already taken place in our economy just waiting to take advantage of free trade.
Some of this was put together before free trade in order to deal with the European and Japanese competition. It is in place. It wants free trade in order to be fully effective.
Lower prices for intermediate goods will make Canadian industries much more competitive as well, and let us not forget that. That, too, will create jobs not only in Canada and in the U.S. but in overseas markets as well. With a greatly enlarged market for Canadian goods, production in Canada could expand by almost 3.5 per cent by the time the agreement is fully implemented.
Among our industrial sectors, the favourable impact will naturally be largest for manufacturing. It used to be that that sector that was the weakest in Canada. It is here under free trade that there will be the best opportunities to take advantage of the economies of scale, and by the time the agreement
June 21, 1988

is fully implemented, Canada's manufacturing output should grow by about 11 per cent, according to the Department of Finance study's conservative projection. Even Canada's more highly protected industries can gain from the progressive elimination of tariffs.
It is quite right to stop and look at our industries that are sheltered behind high tariffs. What is going to happen to them? Well, these industries will gain because these are the same industries that tend to be highly protected on the other side of the border.
Petrochemicals are a very, very good example. Six of the 10 most protected industries in each country are common to both, and the remainder are in similar industrial categories. For many industries, tariff reductions will leave their relative competitive positions largely unaffected, but I would predict that huge American tariffs against our petrochemical exports are going to be removed in five years. In 10 years, this is going to be a bonanza for the petrochemical valley of the Sarnia area.
Our study shows that real income would rise by about 2.5 per cent once the economy is fully adapted to the free trade agreement, and this represents a permanent increase in real income of $12 billion in today's dollars. This is equivalent to a permanent real income gain of about $1,800 for a Canadian household of four, and this is not a one-time gain. This will be there year after year after year. That is what it means to the average Canadian household.
The free trade agreement is good in these macro economic senses, but it is also good for the different regions and provinces of Canada. The Atlantic region with its smaller manufacturing sectors will gain substantially because of the lower prices of manufactured goods purchased from other regions of Canada as well as the U.S. The FTA will also give greater scope for the further processing of resources. The fishery, food processing and resource-based industries, in particular, stand to benefit considerably. Now the Americans are quite happy to take the raw fish. Removing their tariffs on processed fish will allow us to do that processing. Trade liberalization will not only protect these industries and protect these jobs, but it will open the door to new opportunities and further expansion. That is the basic message.

Ontario and Quebec will gain through the increased and more secure access to the large U.S. market which will create more opportunities for investment and will allow their industries to reap the benefits of specialization and large scale production.

The energy agreement creates exciting new opportunities for western development. We know how keen westerners are on oil, natural gas, uranium and hydro electricity. Enhanced and more secure access to U.S. markets will allow the prairie
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
provinces finally to really secure their export opportunities in the U.S. and to enhance them.
Further benefits will be gained as well through diversified growth of agricultural exports on the prairie provinces, and in a similar fashion the economy of British Columbia will benefit from increased opportunities. Tariff reductions will make mineral exports more competitive in the U.S. market. These reductions will increase the scope for further processing of minerals and other resource-based products.
Free trade will lead to more processing. That is also something that all Canadians have been hoping for. There is a great deal of appreciation, therefore, in all parts of the country of the benefits of the agreement, but there have also been misconceptions that the agreement is somehow not good for Ontario. I want to take just a moment to deal with this issue.
Ontario enjoys the advantages offered by quite a diverse economy. It has a strong manufacturing sector and a strong industrial sector in addition to well developed farming and natural resource sectors. It has a very balanced economy as a whole. "Booming" is the adjective that is used most often to describe Ontario's economy. A good part of the reason for this boom is the fact that Ontario has highly developed trade relations with the United States. We cannot deny that Ontario has deep relationships with the United States in terms of trade, and that has helped to produce this boom.
In recent years, all of this has had a cloud over it because of the threat of protectionism. Ontario has already experienced first-hand the pinch of U.S. protectionism, for example, in steel products. Protectionism results in lost jobs, weakened competitive abilities, higher prices and restricted growth. No Ontarian, no Canadian, no political leader regardless of political Party can remain indifferent to the threat of U.S. protectionism, least of all Ontario. Securing access to the U.S. markets and removing all tariffs between the two countries by 1998 augurs very well for many sectors of Ontario economy and particularly for the development of an even stronger, more competitive manufacturing sector.
I want to underline in this regard that the Auto Pact will be made stronger by the free trade agreement. If there is a spine that runs through the Ontario economy, it is the Auto Pact. With the conclusion of this agreement, auto workers, auto parts suppliers, automobile companies and consumers in both countries will benefit greatly from the liberalization of trade in this sector.
Since its inception 22 years ago, the Auto Pact has been subject to review and cancellation upon one year's notice. We cannot forget this. The Auto Pact will not be there forever. It can be cancelled in one year. By wrapping the free trade agreement around the Auto Pact, it has been preserved. It cannot be cancelled now without cancelling the FTA itself. Indeed, the agreement will expand free trade to include new sectors in the industry, replacement parts and tires.

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Resource-Dependent Northern Ontario in particular has not always been able to share fully in the overall health of the Ontario economy. The reduction of tariffs, particularly of finished products, will help reverse that situation. It will expand export opportunities and provide increased scope for further processing in Canada of resource-based products.

Ontario farmers, whose output is the largest of all the provinces, will benefit by more secure access to U.S. markets. At the same time, the interests of the dairy, poultry, fresh fruit and vegetable producers have been safeguarded in this agreement and many more sectors stand to benefit as new opportunities arise to do business in the largest and richest market in the world, and that means new growth and new jobs.
We have also worked out something very interesting for all provinces, but especially for Ontario, a new code to cover trade in services, the first international agreement to accomplish this. At present, Canada's service industries employ 70 per cent of our labour force and are concentrated in Ontario. We know that the province is particularly strong in telecommunications, engineering, computer services, management consulting, insurance, and banking.
This is very important. When we think of trade we think of trucks filled with goods being taken across the border, but trade is also people with briefcases and training who can give advice, repair a product, or set it up. That will also be part of a new code for freer trade under this agreement. Much of Canada's future employment opportunities will spring from this service sector. Ensuring free trade in services will be crucial in providing further opportunities for people in all parts of the country.
Finally, I want to underline the fundamental importance of investment for the future of the Canadian economy. With or without the free trade agreement, Canadian business and industry can be competitive with the best in the world only by upgrading its capacity to produce high quality goods and services at an attractive price.
The key to improving that capacity is investment. The free trade agreement provides a powerful incentive for that. Many of the benefits which will flow from this free trade Bill are implicit in its provision. However, let us be clear that it is the response of Canadians to new opportunities that will determine just how successful this agreement will be. It is equally clear from the overwhelmingly positive response of Canadian business people that they are more than ready to meet the challenge.
Some opposition Members have made clear that they do not share the Government's confidence in this. They have not listened to the millions of confident Canadians who believe in their own ability to make the most of their opportunities. To
those Members I say, look more closely at what Canadians have accomplished in the past three and a half years.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to my hon. friend's question. He asks probing and serious questions which deserve a serious and extensive set of answers.
First, with regard to the currency, the study done by the Department of Finance pivoted, I believe-although I will have to get this verified-around an 80 or 85 cent dollar. He is asking what would happen to our competitiveness with the United States if the Canadian dollar went up higher. If he is suggesting that we should have a 50, 60, or 70 cent dollar secured forever, he will find very little support in Windsor or elsewhere for such a proposal.
In the first quarter of this fiscal year investment in Canada has been at record breaking heights. It was up by 17 per cent on an annualized basis in the first quarter. That is because of the great confidence people have in the Canadian economy. That means as well that we are importing more. As a matter of fact, our imports were up by 1.3 per cent over the first quarter of the previous year as compared with exports in which there was more than a 3 per cent increase over the first quarter of the previous year.
That has happened because there is so much confidence in our economy and our export performance is so strong that our dollar is strengthening. If free trade is a great success for Canada, the dollar will continue, little by little, to strengthen. This will, of course, be in relationship to the rest of the world. As we strengthen in relation to the rest of the world we can do what the Hon. Member has often told me we should do, that is, export outside of North America and be competitive against the rest of the world. Therefore, the strengthened Canadian currency is a result of confidence in the Canadian economy and nothing else.
The Member tied regional trading blocks to the issue of currency. He tried to create a scare by saying that we are trying to create a regional trading block which will eventually lead to a fixed currency vis-a-vis the United States. That is a hypothesis so remote that it really does not deserve an answer. First, we are not a market. We are not even negotiating a common market. The Hon. Member knows that the Common Market allows the free flow of labour and other elements of production besides goods and services. We are not negotiating that, and they do not even have fixed currencies among them. We are three or four steps from that.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
The Hon. Member refers to the Americans. One moment they will believe the Canadian dollar is too low and the next they will say that it is too high. The Hon. Member may quote the President of Coca-Cola but he could quote someone else with a different view another month. They change, depending on the predicament they are facing. They do not want a Canadian dollar pegged to the American dollar. The Hon. Member could find just as many Americans, if not more, giving the opposite advice from what the Hon. Member just quoted.
The Hon. Member asked about Auto Pact cancellation. I listened carefully to him because he is from Windsor and has an interest in the Auto Pact. I noticed that he did not criticize too much what we have negotiated. He was somewhat worried about the rules of origin, but he did not mention that the rules of origin regulation will be on a stricter basis which, in fact, increases the amount of North American content.
It is also very interesting to note that he said the free trade agreement can be cancelled with six months' notice and therefore the Auto Pact is less safe than it was. He is admitting that the Auto Pact could be cancelled with one year's notice. The free trade agreement, which the Hon. Member has said will develop long-term structural relationships in this economy, will be very hard to change. That is what gives it much more permanence than six months. The Auto Pact is as secure as one could want, with its being included in the free trade agreement.
The Hon. Member asks about the Auto Pact in general. There is no doubt that this agreement improves upon the Auto Pact. We stated in the special joint committee report that we do not want the Auto Pact weakened. It is strengthened. I do not believe the Hon. Member is against strengthening the Auto Pact, which is what we have done.
