During his speech the Minister carefully avoided saying how this trade deal will affect Canadian wine producers, how it will affect shoe and textile workers, and how it will affect the computer industry. More important, the Minister failed to address the basic issues that have been put on the table in discussing the trade deal itself.
It seems to me that the trade deal is a test of credibility of politicians in the first place. The House will recall the statements made in 1983 by two important political figures then and, even more important, now. They were the Leader of the Official Opposition and the finance critic at that time, both of whom took a position that has been widely quoted here and in other places in opposition to any trade deal with the United States. Therefore, this very debate includes a test of the credibility of politicians who take a stand in the opposition and

reverse it 180 degrees when in power. What does that do to public opinion about our action? It certainly has an impact.
Second, the debate on the trade deal is one on values we hold dear as a society and as Canadians. On the one hand there is the mind set that only understands the dollar sign, as demonstrated this afternoon by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) in his speech. Nothing else counts except economic performance. That is the philosophical position that he and members of his Cabinet adhere to and which they have embraced in advancing this Bill.
The other side of the debate in dealing with Bill C-130 is not a question of the economy but a question of sovereignty. It is whether Canadians would hold more dear the notion of the dollar value or the value of sovereignty. That will be the test when we judge the very essence of this measure in the next election. The sooner there is an opportunity to do so by way of an election, the better. It is absolutely essential that this matter be debated and voted upon by Canadians during the next election, in light of the lack of credibility in statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), when they were in opposition.
Third, this debate on free trade puts before Canada a fundamental choice: The choice between going the route of continentalism as a nation, which has been rejected on a number of occasions in the last decades, or taking the multilateral trade path that allows us the advantages of trade through the GATT system with all nations of the globe.

In the limited time available I will have to concentrate on the environment. It was in January, 1986 that the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council raised some questions with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). The trade deal was just in its infancy at that time. It made some seven points, and I will briefly put them on record because they are interesting. These issues were raised, but they were never dealt with by the Government.
First, the council said there is an obligation for public consultation, input and education on the environmental implications of freer trade and the negotiations on which actions should be taken. What was done with that recommendation? Nothing. The council went on to say that there are no readily available comparative data on environmental standards and regulations in Canada and the United States and on the levels of implementation. It said that there is a need for comparative data on other environmental management programs, and urged that these be developed and established. This recommendation went by unnoticed.

Fourth, an expanded set of environmental principles was suggested by the council, which could be accepted and used as a guide by the negotiating teams during bilateral and multilateral negotiations. That recommendation went unheeded.
Fifth, the council said that to ensure that Canada's essential environmental concerns are protected, the Canadian negotiating team should be provided with a list of environmental non-negotiables. That was an eminently good suggestion which was not dealt with. It would have removed a number of anxieties and uncertainties that still exist here in this Chamber today. While the Government found it necessary to exempt beer, unprocessed fish and lumber, it did not include water in the exemptions. That is why we have this enormous question mark with respect to water. June 21, 1988

discussions on the environmental implications of freer trade by the Canadian Council of Resource and Environmental Ministers. Unfortunately, and it is highly regrettable, all the suggestions contained in the report by the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council, which is now two and a half years old, went by unnoticed. What happens then? We examine the document which is now the object of our debate and we find, for instance, a chapter on pesticides. In that reference to pesticides in the trade deal, the word "harmonization" pops up several times. It is given an important position because there has to be eventually a coming together of regulations and standards. But the word "harmonization" is loose and floating in the air because no one knows how to interpret it. What does "harmonization of pesticides" mean? I am inclined to agree with the view expressed by the Canadian Environmental Law Association in Toronto. In its issue of November-December it states, on the question of harmonization of standards, that, given the greater size and power of the United States Government and industry lobbyists, the standards to be set are more likely to serve American interests than Canadian. The negotiation of the deal, with no consideration of the environmental impacts, can give us no confidence in our Canadian negotiators' ability to hang tough in the face of any future American pressures to reduce our standards where they are higher. Nor should we rely on them to institute new standards to protect our particular environment. Further, who will decide and on what criteria which U.S. goods meet the objectives of Canadian environmental standards?
These questions could have been dealt with and answered in a satisfactory manner, I submit, if the report of the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council had been heeded and implemented at the time it was put to the Minister over two years ago.
Also with respect to the environment, we asked at the time of Estimates a number of questions of the officials from the Department. Unfortunately, it turned out that they were given no leadership by the Minister. They were left alone to decide whether or not and to what extent there will be environmental impacts as a result of the trade deal. Therefore, the net consequence of that lack of leadership has been the fact that Environment Canada has not carried out one study, not even an internal study, to determine what will be the net effect of the trade deal on our natural resources, on our environmental standards, on our assessment procedures and on the pollution control measures that at the present time exist in Canada and which could come under pressure once the agreement becomes law.
The situation is so bad that in the January-February issue of the Network News by the Ontario Environmental Network publication, I find the following subtitle: "We are to become the suppliers of the raw materials which Americans need,

having depleted many of their own resources". This is a commentary, of course, on the implications of the sharing of natural resources, which may be criticized, perhaps, but nevertheless is the result of the darkness in which Canadians have been left over time on questions of such importance, particularly those who are keen and active in the field of the environment.
Time forces me to move on and deal specifically with the question of energy. I was really hoping the Minister of State for Finance would still be here. He denied that under this trade deal we would be entering North American energy markets in which we will be giving away our natural resources in such an unheard of manner. I am quoting from a publication that came out of Edmonton published by the Council of Canadians on February 11, 1988. "What a foolish strategy to abandon our ability to attract new jobs and new investment through new petrochemical plants, fertilizer plants, chemical plants, and the attracting of new energy-intensive industry. All other countries in the world use their energy for a comparative advantage to attract new business and create new jobs and to diversify their economies".
"How ridiculous to say that we are now going to continue to sell energy below replacement cost. How absurd to agree to supply non-Canadians even if Canadians run short. How nonsensical to weaken our tests for Canadian long-range energy needs. How preposterous to abandon the aspirations for establishing a self-reliant trade policy. How utterly irresponsible to say that our elected Government can no longer charge fees to produce higher revenue for export of energy. How ridiculous to sign an agreement to guarantee the pro rata export of hundreds of thousands of barrels of fine quality, accessible, low-cost Alberta crude, and accept a firm limit of 50,000 barrels a day of unusable Alaska sludge in return".
"How foolish to abandon energy pricing as a means of aiding regional development in Canada, or to abandon the ability to have a two-price energy policy, one for domestic consumers and another for export. How nonsensical to bargain away the control of our natural resources in return to access to a market that will soon be pleading for more Canadian energy".
That is quite a list of relevant questions that the Government has not even started to address in this debate. I am looking forward to hearing from the western Conservative Members in tackling that position.
It is therefore no wonder that at this stage there are Canadians who are developing a resistance to this trade deal, a group of concerned Canadians which consists of people such as retired public servant Ed Gallant; George Ignatieff, the former Ambassador to the UN and Chancellor of the University of

Toronto; John Halstead, a career diplomat who served as our Ambassador to West Germany and NATO; Roger Guindon, a former director of Ottawa University; Yves Dube, former Dean of Social Science at Laval; Louis Blanchard, Director of the University of Moncton; Wallace McCain of McCain Foods, Farley Mowatt; and Mel Clark. What we are debating here is not a trade deal. We are here debating whether or not Canada should become integrated in North America and become part of a North American continental policy at the expense of the alternative that we have advanced in our Party, namely, a global approach, an approach that would enhance our capacity to reach out globally and not just within one continent.
Of course, to do that we need a national economic strategy, something which I am sure my colleagues in the course of debate will advance, flesh out and thus demonstrate that there is an alternative for Canada. The one that is being proposed by the present Government is not the road to go, namely, to withdraw behind the walls of fortress North America and abandon the rest of the globe, creating the impression that in North America alone lies our future. We are already sufficiently dependent on trade with the United States. If anything, we should find ways of expanding our interests and putting our eggs in many more baskets. We should ensure first and foremost that we do not abandon our capacity to define and determine our economic and political destiny.
This Bill is infringing upon the future of our capacity to make decisions that affect our independence and our ability to determine our future as a nation. In that sense, we would be committing a very serious mistake by adopting it.

Mr. Speaker, I simply cannot let my friend get away with some of those comments, which were really quite outrageous. He knows better in his own mind. He surely remembers that the Depression of the 1930s was not really brought on by the climatic disaster we faced in the West. It was brought on when the United States Congress put tariffs up by over 40 per cent. Every other country in the world had to respond. Everyone was impoverished. In this country there were tens of thousands of young men and women who travelled back and forth across the country because they could not get a job. Why could they not get a job? Because no one could afford to purchase products. In 1935, Canada and the United States signed the agreement that started to reduce those tariffs. Jobs started to be created. The war came along. After the war we got into GATT.
The tariffs have moved from over 40 per cent down to something in the order of 9 per cent, which is now the average Canadian tariff. Every time we reduced those tariffs, more Canadians went to work.
The magic of trade between nations is that the wealth of everyone rises. It is during that reduction of those tariffs that we have generated enough wealth in the country that this Parliament could make independent sovereign decisions to bring in medicare, family allowances, social welfare programs and all sorts of regional development programs. The wealth of every Canadian has increased as a result of that.
The reality is that the U.S. Congress is becoming more and more protectionist. Everyone acknowledges that. If it drives those tariffs up again, we will lose jobs. It is one thing to say that we might go into a global situation, and I would like my friend to comment on that, but the fact of the matter is that the world is coming increasingly under trading blocs, pursuant to GATT. It is legal under GATT for two or more nations to get into a free trade agreement. Seventy-one nations in the world have got into free trade agreements. Not one has ever backed out of a free trade agreement. In every instance the smaller nation has benefited more than the greater one.

I have one comment to make. In the environment field I want to assure my friend that Canada's ability to introduce environmental standards has not been affected by the FT A. I will not go on because I do not want to abuse my privilege to comment. However, I could get into the energy sector and

show my friend how it was that his Party, which destroyed tens of thousands of jobs in western Canada as a result of an ill-conceived national energy policy, was not prepared to put on its own people in Ontario and Quebec in terms of electricity. speechtext:
I was listening with keen interest to the dissertation of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and the twisting of the ideals of free trade. We are supposed to be retreating into continentalism, or within our continent. We are not. We are ensuring that we do not lose trade in order that hundreds and hundreds of wood workers in British Columbia do not lose their jobs. We are endeavouring to agree on free trade and assured trade with the Americans so that we can work together with the Americans. They are our greatest customer, despite our greatest efforts to trade with the European Economic Community, Japan, the Pacific Rim, and China. In China we are increasing our trade, but we are having difficulties because of the protectionism within the European Economic Community. In some areas we are trading less. We are working harder than ever to trade with them. But at the same time let us not be blind and let us not think negatively about our greatest trading partner, the wealthiest country in the world.
As a Government we would be doing a disservice to the people of Canada if we, through looking far away, forgot our neighbour, overlooked our neighbour, and did not appreciate the fact that it has the wealth, the desire, the ability, and the need for Canadian products. Whether those products are manufactured in central Canada, or whether they are national resources, natural gas, oil, gasoline, petrol products from the West, lumber from Alberta, British Columbia, and from the central provinces, the Americans want them. They are asking for them. Why should we turn away from that?
The Hon. Member talks of the environment. In the last four years we have done more for the environment together with the Americans in a positive manner. We have worked hard. In November, 1987, the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement was renewed. The federal Government of Canada, the Government of the United States, the New York State Government, and the Ontario Government signed an agreement toward resolving the problem of toxic chemicals in the Niagara River. Two months later the Government announced a series of Canada-U.S. bilateral measures to deal with the problems caused by the high level of the Great Lakes.
We are constantly working with our neighbours for the betterment of Canada, for the betterment of the United States,

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
for the betterment of all peoples here. It is important that we work together. We have and they need, therefore this trade is essential. The free trade agreement between the United States and Canada will solidify prosperity in Canada through increased trade.
Any country that trades is successful. Any country that trades becomes richer. We want to ensure the existence of this trade. That is why the Hon. Member knows, deep down, that without trading with the Americans, Canada will lose over one million jobs. I ask the Hon. Member, why does he not admit that free trade is better than what he is suggesting, global trade with people who cannot afford our products and who do not buy? This is where we trade. We want assured trade, and that is what this is all about.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the so-called free trade agreement, Bill C-130, is a debate about the future of our country. It is a debate as to whether we will continue as an independent and distinctive country with the powers and capacity to make the decisions we want to make to control our environment, natural resources, culture and social programs and to provide jobs for Canadians from coast to coast and stimulate development in regions that have high rates of unemployment. It is about our capacity to make our decisions ourselves.
In effect, Bill C-130 is a constitutional amendment that itself cannot be amended and that will change the course of our history for the rest of time. Yet it is not being debated as such, it is being disguised as simply a trading arrangement with our American partners.
Many church groups, unions, voluntary organizations, women's groups and environmentalists have protested this trade deal. I simply want to refer to a statement made by one such group, the Anglican Church of Canada, incidentally my own church, which I think symbolizes very well what is at the core of what is wrong with this trade agreement. Four points were made in the Anglican Church's condemnation of the free trade agreement and its urging of federal reassessment of it.
Economic plans must not affect negatively the most vulnerable members of our Canadian society or of our global family.
Surely it is the most vulnerable who will be affected, the people in regions which are economically underdeveloped and the people who depend vitally on social programs.
Economic or social agreements should not be undertaken if they limit society's members from making future decisions on behalf of the common good.
We will be limited in the decisions that we can make in the future and certainly limited in the decisions we can make for the common good, because it will not be our society through our elective representatives who will make these decisions. It will be market forces and dispute settlement panels.
Economic agreements should not be undertaken which reduce our ability as a society to be good stewards of our environment and rich heritage of natural resources.
There are serious environmental implications in the agreement. Natural resources including non-renewable resources will be treated as ordinary commodities, as widgets to be traded across our borders. They will not be regarded as part of our heritage, part of the environment that must be protected and over which future generations have a very reasonable and just claim.
Finally,
ordinary citizens must be allowed an opportunity to understand what is at stake and to take part in a meaningful way in decisions of major importance.
That too is one of the aspects of the betrayal in this trade deal. Ordinary Canadians have not had the opportunity to understand this. Even the Premiers were deceived about vital aspects of the so-called trade arrangement.
People have not had a chance to go over the agreement. It is complicated. It requires books and books and appendices and appendices. The Government of Canada has not dealt squarely with Canadians. It has hidden the deal by calling it one that is merely about trade. It turned out to be not just about trade in goods but also in energy, investment, culture, services and social programs.
It is about how the federal and provincial Governments will or will not get along together, because in future, if the trade deal goes through, it will be the federal Government that will be bossing the provinces and municipalities and enforcing the trade agreement on behalf of the United States, the other party to the agreement. The federal Government will be forcing compliance on the provincial, municipal and territorial Governments. Indeed, if there is ever Indian self-government, Indians too will be affected because all these rights are given away in this shameless deal called the free trade agreement.
June 21, 1988

One of the worst parts of this deal is the part dealing with energy. That is one of the surprises in the deal. People did not know that continental energy would be part of the arrangement. It was supposed to be a deal involving manufactured goods and other ordinary subjects of trading arrangements that other countries have entered into. It was certainly not supposed to be about continental energy.
Even some of the advocates of the trade deal are worried about energy supply. The Ontario Natural Gas Association favours the trade deal because it can see that there will be opportunities to make money of it. We know that the owners and suppliers have interests which are very different from those of the consumers, just as the banks love service charges, but are they good for consumers? Money that can be made by selling non-renewable resources as a commodity is certainly to the advantage of the companies, but it is not to the advantage of consumers and it is certainly not to the advantage of young Canadians who will have to grow older in a very cold climate and in a country that needs its fuel resources very badly.
This advocate of the deal, the Ontario Natural Gas Association, nonetheless points out what the disadvantages of it are for Canadians. In effect, while the National Energy Board retains the authority to review export applications and to identify potential inequities or market anomalies, its ability to act appears to be severely limited. Once we start selling it, we will have to keep selling it. Proportionate reduction of this supply is permitted, but proportionate reduction is not quite as proportionate as one might think.
Canada now supplies approximately 5 per cent of the total natural gas consumption in the United States, whereas virtually the entire Canadian market is dependent on domestic supply. A 10 per cent reduction in natural gas supplies would affect fully 10 per cent of the Canadian market compared with only 0.6 per cent of the United States market in national terms. If we have to conserve our resources because of some kind of crisis, it would be only fair to cut back proportionately. It will not be fair, though. The cut-back for Canadians is very much greater than it is for Americans because they have other suppliers. We can hurt ourselves, but they will be largely untouched. It is a deal that is very much to their advantage but not to the advantage of Canadians.
In effect, the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement creates a North American market for natural gas. The U.S. currently has a 10-year reserves-to-production ratio, while Canada has 30 years. If the United States has equal, unfettered access to Canadian supplies, the result is a combined 13-year ratio. We do not believe Canadians have yet realized that their natural gas supply security margin could overnight be more than cut in half, and this Government has not been square with Canadians and told them that.
The same could be said for conventional oil. I will not go into that example because there is not time, but that is a disaster too. Canadians do not know that the supply we have is
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
a very fragile one and it will not last or we will have to go very much farther afield to areas which are much more difficult to work in.
The association says that it does not believe that sufficient consideration has been given to the impact of a rapid increase in the number of long-term, large volume contractual arrangements. This is a very serious matter indeed. Potential shortfalls could occur by the close of this decade. Has the Government talked to Canadians fairly about that? Yet we are treating this as an unlimited supply of a resource that we want to give away cheaply.
Another aspect of betrayal that Canadians did not know was in the trade deal and had to find out by reading the fine print over a period of time had to do with water. Water is not supposed to be in the trade deal, we were told by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). He said, before the full text had been revealed: "The subject of water has never been negotiated in the free trade talks. The subject of water is not part of the free trade agreement, nor will it be". However, water is in the free trade agreement. Article 409 says that once you start to export a good you have to continue to export it. Anyone who begins to export will be obligated to continue.
The schedule to the trade agreement, Tariff Item 22.02, includes waters. The Minister responsible for International Trade tries to make a joke of it and make it sound as though we were only talking about soda water and fizzy pop. That is not so. We are talking about regular water; rivers, lakes, tankers full of water, water that we very badly need as well.
Once a mistake is made it cannot be unmade. One of the very bad parts of this deal is that it freezes those kinds of decisions. Instead of the situation of having a government which can be thrown out and replaced by another government which will change the policy, this decision will be permanent.
This is a subject about which I think our Liberal friends ought to be a little embarrassed because they have talked rather freely about the desirability of water exports and water in the trade deal. This is a subject absolutely vital to our environment. Yet there is no provision in the trade deal for protecting our water sources for purposes of protecting the environment. That is not allowed. It will be treated as any other ordinary commodity.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-130 is no ordinary Bill. It is an amendment to the Canadian Constitution. This amendment affects twenty-seven Acts of Parliament. It is an amendment that involves a reduction in powers at the federal, provincial and municipal levels. The federal Government, which is party to the agreement, will become the U.S. Administration's agency for implementing the agreement.
The Premier of Quebec favours the FTA. He says that his Government will make the requisite legislative amendments,

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
and that the federal Government would not have to force him to do so. But what do we do tomorrow, about free trade and the present Quebec Government's policies? If these change, what do we do? The FTA constitutes a freeze on political change in this country. Once that choice is made, we can no longer make any changes. However, a government has no right to tie down future governments.
It is antidemocratic. People should have the right to replace a government and its policies with another government and other policies, something that would no longer be possible after the FTA is signed. The federal Government, supported by the Province of Quebec, will tie all future governments: federal, provincial and municipal. The issues involved are important and include energy, investment, culture, social programs and regional economic development. What if a Quebec government wants to launch a social program? What if it wants to promote economic development in a disadvantaged region? It would have to ask the federal Government to make new representations to the U.S. Administration. We would have to consider whether the proposed development constituted unfair subsidies under the terms of the agreement. This is against the level playing field principle. We would have to consider whether the measure constituted a monopoly prohibited under articles 2010 and 2011.
In that case, economic retaliatory measures by the United States are to be expected. Or the province may be ordered to compensate the U.S. companies involved for their loss of business, including any future losses. In any case, it won't be Quebec or Canada that will decide but the Canada-U.S. Trade Commission. Canada does not have a majority on this Commission, and Quebec would not be represented.
The sovereignty of Quebec is endangered along with Canadian sovereignty. Any government will lose the power to make decisions for its citizens. It would be a victory for the private sector and its values and a defeat for the people and the values of our society, especially social solidarity.
With the Meech Lake Accord, Quebec will again join the Canadian Constitutional family. How ironic! Quebec is joining the Constitution at the same time as the Constitution is being weakened by free trade. The men and women of Quebec must say no to this Agreement with the United States. We say yes to Meech Lake, yes to cooperation between the federal Government and Quebec and no to selling out our political sovereignty to the Americans!

This is profoundly a question of constitutional change. I think the Attorney General of Ontario put it very well in his analysis of the impact of the deal. He said:
What does this mean to federal-provincial relations within Canada? The agreement threatens our traditional system in part by inserting a third party, the United States, with the right to insist on legal solutions to problems of economic regulation, problems that Canadians have tended to settle among themselves without recourse to legal remedies ... The present agreement may effectively require that many provincial policies be approved by the United States before they are put in effect.
That is a shocking intrusion into the normal way in which we conduct ourselves in this country, the normal, co-operative arrangements with which we have achieved all of our social programs-sitting down, negotiating, and figuring out something which suits Canadians and Canadian conditions. I quote further:
The free trade agreement between Canada and the United States has an extensive impact on the power of the provinces to control their economy. This impact is not merely incidental or temporary but involves a systematic reduction of the freedom of Canadians to make policy.
As a consequence, the agreement effects a change of constitutional dimensions in federal-provincial relations in Canada, even though it does not touch the wording of the Constitution ... The ability of the United States to insist on legal rights where Ottawa and the provinces have often compromised and co-operated fundamentally alters the Canadian tradition.
That is what is so profoundly wrong with this agreement. It changes how we do things. It changes the Canadian way, the way of solidarity, the way of co-operation. We do not want the law of the jungle. We do not want legal remedies and market forces determining everything. We do not want American crime rates. We cannot have it both ways. If we want to have our kind of society, we have to pay the price, and we have done so with our social programs. You cannot have the law of the jungle and do it that way.
I am sorry to say that there have not yet been any Conservatives who have bolted from the caucus. There have not been any who remember the Canada of Sir John A. Macdonald, the Canada of using the state creatively to find solutions to our problems. That has not happened.
However, I appeal to Conservatives across the country who did not vote for this Government in order to give it a mandate to bring in free trade, to Conservatives who love their country, to realize that it must now be saved by throwing out the Government. The Government is not going to vote free trade down. It has the power and is using closure. It is going to get free trade through. Perhaps the Senate will slow the process down, but the Government, with no mandate to do so, nonetheless has the power to change our Constitution forever if it gets away with it.
I hope that many Conservatives will regret the decision they made to bring in this Government. I hope they will see the betrayal of trust in so many ways, in patronage, lack of honesty, and lack of openness in all of these respects. I hope that these Canadians will want to keep Canada Canadian and will change their vote in the next election.
When they are deciding between the Liberals and the New Democrats I urge them to be very careful because the Liberals are not so sure about where they stand on trade. A former Liberal Minister of Finance was one of the instigators of it, and the Liberals in Quebec are supporting it actively. If Canadians want to be sure that this deal is defeated, they must support the New Democratic Party because we will tear up this deal.
In a few seconds remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, let me say that this is a profound decision about the future of our
June 21, 1988

country. We are not urging that the status quo remain. We are talking about having the power and the ability to change and to adapt to changing conditions. The world is changing and we must change in response to it. However, we must have the power to do that. This free trade Bill, C-130, takes those powers away from the federal and the provincial Governments. We must defeat the free trade deal, if not in the House, at the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with rapt interest as the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) gave her dissertation about her Party's view of what they believe Canada should be like. I share her concern that we must look after our social programs.
The previous government, together with the New Democratic Party, gave us many social programs and spent money like it was water under the bridge. As our deficit ever increased, they never said how they would pay for their programs.
Our Government agrees that we need social programs, but we will pay for them. In the last Budget we were a fraction of a percentage point within paying for all our debts, including all our social programs. We can only look after our social programs with strength, trade, good management and employment. We cannot pay for our social programs with wishful thinking or myopic views whereby we look after ourselves and no one can touch us. We will only be vassals of the Americans if we are weak and think only of ourselves.
We have proven that we are stronger today than ever before as a result of good management of the economy which this Government is providing for the first time in 40 years. We can address all the concerns the Hon. Member has raised by good management, and a free trade agreement that allows greater trade with the strongest nation in the world, the United States.
The Hon. Member's figures dealing with energy are fictitious. We have more oil reserves in Alberta than all the Middle East combined. A 30 or 40-year oil supply is a figment of her imagination. We have enough oil in Alberta itself to supply the United States and Canada until our grandchildren are grandmothers and grandfathers. We only have to develop it and sell it. Furthermore, we control what we sell. It is only given away if we are weak and myopic. Nothing is given away by this free trade agreement. It is a guarantee to provide our citizens with prosperity and the opportunity to work while controlling our destiny.
The Hon. Member talked about social programs and energy. We need to provide leadership through knowledge, and good business and labour management so that Canadians will have confidence that we can trade effectively not only with the Americans but with the rest of the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have seldom heard such nonsense in many of the points that were made. I will attempt to answer them.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
The Hon. Member talked about controlling the deficit when, in fact, there are still deficits in the area of $30 billion in Conservative budgets every year. A good example of social programs and deficit control is CCF and NDP Saskatchewan governments which pioneered social programs and reduced the public debt. They proved it is possible to have humane and fair government while balancing the budget. I challenge anyone to follow the example of Tommy Douglas and his successors there.
The Hon. Member talked about oil. My examples concerned natural gas and social programs because I only have 20 minutes in this debate to talk about the future of Canada. One cannot cover all the issues. While I chose to talk about natural gas, oil is another question.
The Hon. Member believes that there is an ample supply of oil. That may be true when one includes such far-away places as the Beaufort Sea and other fragile areas in terms of the environment, the tar sands where oil is difficult to retrieve, and oil in the offshore where it may ruin the fishery. The large amounts of oil about which the Hon. Member talks are not readily available.
The Hon. Member said oil would be available until our grandchildren grow up. I remind him that civilizations have lasted for thousands of years and the sun will not burn out for another four billion years. He should not set his sights so short as to say that the oil companies should sell off all the oil in two generations. We are talking about shortages within the next 10 years, which is a dangerous prospect. Although the Hon. Member suggests that there is a lot of easily available energy resources, they are non renewable resources for which even the oil companies predict there will be shortages within the next 10 years.
Even the producer provinces are disadvantaged by this trade deal. The Constitution clearly specifies that these natural resources are under provincial jurisdiction. Yet their right to control these resources is being taken away by this trade deal. They will not have the opportunity to charge lower prices within the province to stimulate economic development and create jobs. They will lose power to create manufacturing while we will be more dependent on selling the resources quickly at the lowest possible price. I suggest that is not a wise use of natural resources.
The Hon. Member brags about social programs. His Party opposed every one of them and only gradually came on board when public opinion polls showed they would be thrown out if they continued to oppose them. Indeed, the Conservatives moved to deindex the family allowance and tried to deindex the Old Age Pension. The Conservatives lost an election over the Old Age Pension because the Senate turned it down. This Conservative Government would have been thrown out if it continued its plan to deindex the Old Age Pension.
Social programs were on the table and were referred to as disciplining monopolies by the Americans. I do not begrudge the Americans their way of operating. The United States is a

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
sovereign country and can do what it wants. However, we have chosen to do things differently in Canada and we have our social programs, including the Old Age Pension, Canada Pension Plan, Family Allowance, unemployment insurance and medicare. We would not have had medicare if a free trade agreement was in place at that time.
Social programs are challenged in several ways. One is the unfair subsidy section of the deal. We will not know for some five to seven years whether the Americans will consider these as fair or unfair subsidies.
They are also challenged under the monopoly section of the free trade deal. I hope other Members will address that aspect, in which provincial governments must beg the federal Government to make representations to the Americans. They may be ordered to compensate American companies for loss of business because profits to corporations are the most important consideration in the free trade deal, not services to people or planning a humane society. If an American corporation will lose money, then it is a violation of the free trade deal. That could interfere with social programs. This free trade agreement is a travesty. It is inhumane and should not be allowed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this evening to take part in a debate that is very important to this country. Free trade with the United States is neither a luxury nor an intellectual exercise. It merely states the obvious. First of all, Quebec sends two-thirds of its exports to the United States. Second, two million jobs depend directly on our trade with our neighbours to the South. Third, our access to this market of 250 million people must be protected and guaranteed by an official and duly-signed agreement.
Of course, our opponents got carried away by their rhetoric. They maintain that we are selling Canada's independence in order to gain access to the U.S. market. Mr. Speaker, Canada exists by the will of its citizens, and we underestimate Canadians if we think their will is particularly vulnerable.
The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was not signed on a whim. It was the fruit of careful negotiations during which we did not give in on essential matters.
The agreement does not put any restrictions on grants to businesses or on regional development. Marketing boards will continue to exist, which means that Canada will retain the right to determine its agricultural marketing programs.
The agreement also provides for a dispute settlement mechanism. As for the adjustments that will be necessary in certain businesses, my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) and I announced the creation of an advisory committee on adjustment last January. Mr. Speaker, the committee chaired by Mr. Jean de Grandpre will ensure that Canadians take advantage of the new opportunities offered by
free trade, while identifying any adjustment problems that may arise.
The agreement signed with the United States provides the catalyst Canadian business needed to go the extra mile and rise to new heights. With the agreement, Canadians and Quebecers have gained secure and permanent access for their products in key sectors, including agriculture, resource processing, manufacturing, energy and services, all of which will be given a fresh boost.
More secure access to the U.S. market will make Canadian industries more dynamic, more innovative and more competitive, because being able to count on access to this market will give investors the necessary confidence to create new companies, consolidate existing ones and meet the competitive challenge.
The economic impact of the FTA has already been assessed. Experts at the Department of Finance predict an increase of 2.5 per cent in the real income of Canadians. This represents $12 billion more in the Canadian economy and the creation of at least 120,000 new jobs over the next five years.
Mr. Speaker, it is up to the investors and the entrepreneurs, to this country's businessmen and women, to make these figures come true.
Free trade is a challenge, not for government, but for all Canadians who will have to make sure they get the most out of this agreement.
Mr. Speaker, for four years Canada's economy has outclassed the economies of all other major industrialized countries in terms of growth and job creation. We want to use free trade to secure the future economic development of this country.
Mr. Speaker, speaking of job creation, I wish to point out that as Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, I am very interested in small and medium-sized business, needless to say. While big corporations have been streamlining their operations for several years now, small and medium-sized businesses have taken up the slack and are the real driving force of the economy throughout Canada. These companies with less than 100 employees account for 99 per cent of all Canadian companies and 70 per cent of jobs created, on average. Furthermore, they generally spend more on research and development, proportionately, than big corporations.
It is therefore not surprising that they can adjust quickly to technological changes and also transform their industrial infrastructure very rapidly if market conditions change suddenly.
So, Mr. Speaker, I listen to small businesses. Naturally, I talk to them about free trade and do you know what they tell me, these men and women who one would think would be vulnerable and afraid? They are eager for tariff barriers to

June 21, 1988

come down completely. They are eager to see a significant reduction in non-tariff barriers. Yes, these men and women want to take on new markets in the United States and then new markets elsewhere. They have been preparing for months to face this new challenge.
These business men and women are looking for new forms of partnership with the Americans, and also with other countries. They are searching for new markets. In short, they are eager to diversify and broaden their customer base.

It is to complete the picture and to ensure access to a market of 250 million consumers. It is to make sure that we can continue to deal with the Americans, and rather than charge into it, we will have 10 years for both sides to adjust.
The complete lowering of tariff barriers will therefore be the end of a long process. The purchasing power of Canadians will gradually increase over the period, by 3 to 12 per cent, according to economists who have estimated the impact of free trade on the standard of living of our fellow citizens.

Again, I would like to summarize briefly the four main objectives of our negotiations with the United States. First, guaranteed access to the U.S. market; second, trade rules that will eliminate improvisation; third, a binational mechanism for speedy settlement of our respective national problems; and fourth, maintaining our institutions that reflect our indentity.
Mr. Speaker, these objectives have been realized. They are the very backbone of the Bill before the House today. These objectives, now that they have been realized, are the cornerstone of the future for generations to come.

Let us forget our differences, and once we have this unprecedented agreement with our most important trading partner, we can legitimately aspire to take our place among world trade leaders. I am convinced that this first step will pave the way for any further developments we may wish to add. Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, depends on today's plans.

I appreciate the Member's question about the notwithstanding clause because it is pretty obvious that, aside from a few Members of the Cabinet, government Members have not bothered to understand the implications behind the notwithstanding clause. As I said in my speech, it is very clear that it is to discourage the creation of similar barriers in third countries. In addition, all subsidies will have to be rethought over the next five to seven years. As I believe the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) once said, the hobnailed boot fell, but only one of the pair.
We were told to be quiet and not to worry for the moment. However, this document from the Congress to the White House indicates very clearly that subsidies are to be negotiated and renegotiated in the energy and cultural sectors. Read the document. I do not understand how government Members cannot read what the Americans are saying.
June 21, 1988

For the sake of my children and my grandchildren I would dearly love to believe them. This is a sixth generation Canadian talking to government Members they are deaf as can be. It says: "extension of the free trade agreement principles to energy and cultural industries to the extent not now covered". It could not be clearer than the noses on their faces if they would only read or look in the mirror.

They include the book publishing development subsidy, the postal rates subsidy, the museum assistance program, the Indian cultural development and art program, the Canada Council program, the Telecom program, funding for the development of our recording industry, public use payment for authors for their works in public libraries, cultural initiative grants, performing arts assistance, capital cost allowance-rotten as that may be right now-and broadcasting subsidies for our public sector. That is why we are in this juggernaut right now.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-130, the Bill which proposes to put into effect the treaty which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) signed at the beginning of the year with the President of the United States. The Bill consists of 123 pages which propose to amend 27 statutes of the Government of Canada ranging from the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Seeds Act, the Meat Inspection Act, the Meat Import Act, the Loan Companies Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Bank Act, the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the Canadian Agricultural Products Standards Act, the Canada Grain Act, the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, and on and on.
The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) described this treaty as a revolution. I believe he is right. It is a neo-Conservative revolution that proposes to turn over our existing society.
The Minister for International Trade is talking about a movement that espouses freedom, as do most revolutionary movements. In this case, however, it is freedom for corporations and multinational firms. It is freedom so that they can get the Government off their backs, become deregulated and take their profits wherever they wish. It is freedom so that they will not be forced to provide services in outlying rural areas of our country, like those I represent. It is freedom so they can make their money wherever they choose, whenever they choose.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
It means privatization so they will not have to compete with government agencies, which they say is unfair competition. Corporations say it is unfair to compete with companies like Air Canada that has the highest return on investment of all three airlines in this country. They want to be able to share in those profits. However, they call for privatization when Crown corporations happen to lose money, using the argument that they cannot compete and will be forced to cut their prices accordingly.
The third leg of the neo-Conservative revolution is tax reform. Corporations have succeeded in convincing many Conservatives that the corporate sector should pay no income tax, using the argument that profits should go to shareholders who should pay the tax. Unfortunately, most developed countries have a practice of maintaining retained earnings, which then become earnings which have virtually no tax. Under those circumstances, large multinational corporations with almost no taxes have a distinct advantage over ordinary business people who try to enter the market and compete against them. The Conservatives are attempting to invert the way the economy functions.
This is a complete change from the economic theories of the western countries in the last 80 years. One of the best examples to describe the system of economic development we have been following is Henry Ford. Just prior to World War I, Henry Ford decided to pay his workers another $1 an hour, something which his competitors and federal industrialists questioned. His workers seemed to have a place to stay warm, seemed not to be too hungry when coming to work, and seemed to have enough clothing. They asked Henry Ford why he would give them more money when they would only waste it or save it. Henry Ford said that they may save the money, but they probably will buy cars with it. He used that theory to increase the amount of cars he sold.
Successive Governments have followed that policy of increasing incomes through such things as the minimum wage, better services to people, better education, health care and standards of living to the benefit of everyone. Productivity and the economy increased and everyone lived better.
The new Conservatism seems to be shifting in the other direction and focusing its attention on reducing labour cost and input costs, avoiding taxation, and turning the economic development strategy on its head. That is what Margaret Thatcher, Ronald Reagan and our Prime Minister are attempting.
The Prime Minister has been following his three tenets of Conservative philosophy: Deregulation, privatization, and tax reform. However, I believe he has been pressured into making this a long-term proposition by corporations who are concerned about what may happen if the Conservatives lose the next election. Their solution was to persuade the Government to sign a free trade agreement with the United States because American Governments have been easier to manipulate than most other Governments, especially those in Canada.

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
When 1 heard the Minister for International Trade this afternoon, I could not help but recall an old A1 Capp comic of L'il Abner because Senator Fogbound immediately came to mind. I remember him thundering: "What is good for General Bullmoose is good for the U.S.". Of course, he was parroting the famous line by one of the big business people of the era who said that what is good for General Motors is good for the United States. It is still true in the United States that what is good for big business is good for the U.S.A., because big business essentially controls the policy of the United States.
If we are linked with the United States through a treaty, then Canada is not very likely to be able to back out of some of the changes the Government has attempted to make. The agreement goes much beyond the removal of a few tariffs between our countries. If that was all there was to it, the hue and cry would be loud and sharp but not so prolonged.
I was told by one analyst that there are 21 segments to this agreement, 11 of which have nothing to do with tariffs. They are more concerned with setting prices, control and deciding the future policy of the country. They have nothing to do with a normal free trade agreement. Rather than reassurance from big business, there are phrases in the Bill, such as those at page 99, which state: "Every reference in those provisions to Canadian shall be read and construed as a reference to American", and "every reference in these provisions to nonCanadian shall be read and construed as a reference to nonCanadian, other than American". There are statements like: "Canadian-controlled shall be read and construed as a reference to American-controlled". It is a blatant attempt to combine the two countries and make American policy, American law and the whole American ethos one with Canada.
The Minister for International Trade said that he was proposing this legislation which he described as a revolution to save the country from stagnation and save it from the New Democratic Party. During Question Period today I heard members of the Government say that there was no stagnation of this country, but that we had a healthy and vibrant economy. The free trade agreement is not even in effect, so what is he fighting against? Perhaps he is fighting against the NDP and against our policy of interfering in the economy for the good of people, so that we can look forward to improving living standards and health care, services and education.
That is what we see with the Japanese and the European economy. Japan probably epitomizes a country that interferes in the economy. It is probably the closest thing to the antithesis of a free trader that exists on the earth at the moment, and who has the leading economy? Who has the highest living standards by most measures right now? It is the Japanese, and many of the European countries are right behind them. By one standard of measuring economic growth I saw recently, the United States was either ninth or tenth, and rested in about the same place in terms of living standard.
Why is it that the Government insists on trying to push us into this particular kind of deal except for ideological reasons which I have spelled out? What is it that it is saving us from? When the Government began these negotiations it said it was saving us from countervail actions. We all recall that there were countervail actions against our softwood lumber, our shakes and shingles, hogs, pork, salt fish, raspberries, specialty steel, potash, and those were just while the negotiations were going on. What did we come out with? Did we get saved from countervail actions such as those? No, we did not. We had the same process in place. We did not change it. But the Government is now happy with the agreement. I wonder why.
The Government told us it was entering into the negotiations to get a better dispute settlement method, that the dispute settlement system had to be changed and improved. Did we get that? No, we did not. We got no change at all. It is the same dispute-settling mechanism with one little change, after it is all over, we can drag it out even longer by putting in a tribunal which will decide whether or not U.S. law was adhered to.
We were told that with these negotiations we would get greater access to the U.S. market. Now that it is all over, is that what is going to happen? Before the negotiations began, we had access on about 80 per cent of our trade, free of tariffs. We had access to most of the U.S. market. If there was an inequity between the access to the American market and their access to our market, it was in our favour because their tariffs were slightly lower than ours. Now that the walls are coming down, it means, by my simple deduction, that they have better access to our market as a result of this agreement. Most people who have spent any time analysing the deal agree.
We have been told the Government had to do it because it was saving Canada for future generations and it just had to stop what was going on. We have been reasonably well off and we seem to be growing quite fast, but the Government has to put a stop to that. It is not good enough. It was stated by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) that this will result in lower cost of consumer goods. Think about it for a moment, Mr. Speaker. Think about the neo-Conservative philosophy that demands and expects lower wage rates, lower resources, access to lower priced raw materials. Why will consumer goods be lower? Most of them are set by oligopolies that generally price what the market will bear. I submit they will be lower because there will be lower demand. People will not have as much money to spend and therefore prices will be lower. Is that such a good thing? I think not.
We have argued with, I think, correctness, according to the agreement after we analysed it, that signing this agreement and approving this legislation will tie us not only closer to the American economy but would subject us to American power, influence and policies. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills (Mr. Thacker), said: "Do not worry. We will still be able to tax ourselves". Hurrah. What good is being able to tax
June 21, 1988

ourselves if we are limited in how we can spend the tax dollars?

Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief. I made a speech on this on an Opposition Day several months ago. At that time I spent most of the full 20 minutes I had describing that. However, I think there are a number of things that disturb me a great deal about the deal as it applies to agriculture.
My friend will be aware that a great many of our agricultural products have been traded freely across the border with the United States, products such as red meats, agricultural implements, chemicals and fertilizers. Quite a number of agricultural items have been traded freely.
Those that were not are those with which we have some disadvantage geographically and, therefore, economically in competing, namely, fruits and vegetables, and poultry and dairy products. Some of the things that our Government proposes to do with this trade agreement are very hard for me to accept.
Show me, Mr. Speaker, another trade agreement wherein a country has guaranteed another country that that other country will be able to ship in "no less than 7.5 per cent", in this case, of the poultry requirements of that country. It is not that there is a window of opportunity there but that it shall be "no less than", and into perpetuity. What a way to stifle economic development in one's own country, to invite in 7.5 per cent of one's own poultry consumption needs from another country and to write that into an international agreement stating that it will never be less than that. It may be more. In fact, it probably will be more if this Government stays in power.
Why put such a thing in an agreement? It is there. We did not get any such reciprocity. Even those in the oil and gas industry who think that this agreement is a good thing because

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
it gives them access to the United States market, which they had, will see that there is not a line in the agreement stating that they will get "no less than 10 per cent" of the total market in the United States. This is utter foolishness and utterly unnecessary.
We have also pretended that marketing boards are not in danger. Yet anyone who thinks ahead or can analyse can realize that there is no way we will be able to maintain the slightly higher prices in our country because of our higher costs and still maintain our processing industry. I think that the McCains have put that very clearly. They have quite publicly stated their options. They have said: "If we are going to make frozen pizzas and frozen chicken dinners with product produced in Canada under supply-management which comes to our factory at a slightly higher rate than what we could get in the United States, then we have no choice but to move our factory, our processing plant into the United States". They go on to state: "Unfortunately, it is easy to move a factory, but it is not easy to move our workers." It is virtually impossible to move our farmers. Thus they will be left sitting there in Florenceville or Portage la Prairie without a factory to haul their product to and there will be no point in their continuing to produce chicken, potatoes or cheese.
Those are the problems with the deal. The Government says that marketing boards are still in place, and they are. However, they will not be able to exist for very long. The Government says that the Wheat Board is still there, and it is. However, the Government has taken away a great many of its powers which kept it a substantial institution which was able to do a good job.
These are some of the items that 1 think have created longterm problems for farmers and about which farmers are very upset.

I am glad the Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills asked that question. It brings out a fact that is sometimes ignored by both sides of this argument.
I have functioned in trading with the United States as a farmer. Even though we had free trade in the commodities that I was trading in it was not any field of roses, so to speak. There were always disputes and tough spots. There were times when one could expect to have one's product stopped at the border. That was with free trade, with an agreement that had been in place for 45 years at that time. The dispute settlement mechanisms have not really changed. The methods that the Americans have to stop this trade have really not changed as a result of this deal.
If we are to be international traders then we have to be prepared to put up with occasional interruptions in trade by the recipient country, whether it is in the United States, Japan, China or the European Economic Community. It does not matter very much whether one is under GATT or a bilateral agreement, these things will happen.
I think the Government fooled itself into thinking that it could improve those minor disruptions and reduce them by signing this agreement. When we analyse what it has got with the agreement, we find it has not got anything any different in reality than what we had before. The words have not improved. They are no stronger than they were before. The process is no different from it was before. All the Government has done is to kid itself that it has something better than it had before. There will still be opportunities for disruptions of trade at the border, at the behest of anyone from pork growers to a feed council to a processor. The U.S. is even more subject to political pressure in terms of its trade policy than we are. That has not changed. Nothing in this agreement can change that.
Congress is not changing its attitude. It is not changing the Constitution or its expectations with respect to what it sees as its role in trade. Thus disruptions will continue to happen after the new agreement comes into effect, or if we stay under the existing agreement. We will have the same problems under the GATT as well. The only advantage under the GATT is that we have an opportunity to form alliances with other members who are being treated by some of the same countries in the same way. We are no longer the only little country dealing with a big country which chooses to act in such a way. We can form alliances with other countries which are similarly affected and eventually we will get some justice.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate of historical significance for the future of both the workers and businessmen of the Louis-Hebert riding as well as for all those who want Canada to have a future consistent with the skills of our people and the industrial, economic and technological potential of our country.
We have before us a bill which faithfully incorporates the elements of the Free Trade Accord which was signed between Canada and the United States. If I may, I should like to point out its purpose:
3. The purpose of this Act is to implement the Agreement, the objectives of which are to
(a)	eliminate barriers to trade in goods and services between Canada and the United States;
(b)	facilitate conditions of fair competition within the free-trade area established by the Agreement;
(c)	liberalize significantly conditions for investment within that free-trade area;
(d)	establish effective procedures for the joint administration of the Agreement and the resolution of disputes; and
(e)	lay the foundation for further bilateral and multilateral cooperation to expand and enhance the benefits of the Agreement.
There is nothing in this bill which was not part of the Agreement signed by the Prime Minister and the President on January 2. We have now reached the turning point. What motives will influence our destiny? Fear and insecurity? Or confidence and a powerful thrust towards the future? That is the choice we have to make. In this debate on free trade we see a confrontation between right wingers and forward looking idealists whose vision of Canada is altogether different.
I can assure you that most people in my riding and my province support the Agreement which was signed between Canada and the United States. Although Quebec City is called the Old Capital, the men and women who live there are not prisoners of the past, they have modern ideas, and they have
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
both the wisdom and good sense to look beyond the old walls surrounding them.
Quebec businessmen are demonstrating a similar openmindedness. For instance, when dealing with free trade, the President of Shermag, the most important Quebec furniture manufacturer, remarked: "It is a matter of attitude: either you freeze or you charge ahead ", Well, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what free trade is offering to our workers and our entrepreneurs, the tools to succeed not only in North America, but also in Europe and in Asia.
We can find that same spirit and confidence everywhere in Quebec. Alain Dubuc, a reporter from La Presse, is a very good example. He stated: "Quebec will greatly benefit from the agreement. We can even say that our province has hit the jackpot." All recent surveys show that a strong majority of Quebecers are in favour of the agreement. Moreover, the results indicate that young people are the most supportive. Why? Because the young people of Quebec are looking to the future, seeking individual freedoms and opportunities on the world market. In fact, we are in the second stage of the Quiet Revolution. In the first stage, Quebecers were able to assert themselves in their own territory.
We have now reached the second stage, the conquest of the foreign markets. In fact, numerous Quebec firms, small and large, are already making progress in the American market and increasingly in Europe and Asia. The confidence Quebecers feel towards the Free Trade Agreement speaks for the maturity and the competence of our entrepreneurs and workers. All those strongly in favour of free trade have realized that we have the economic, technological and industrial capability to take full advantage of a market ten times our own. Moreover, those supporters of free trade know that in order to be recognized as one of the economic and industrial leaders of the world, we need to have privileged access to a market of at least 100 million people. Well, the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States would give us privileged access to a market of 250 million consumers.
Those who would say no to this historic agreement would in fact be turning thumbs down on the growth and competitiveness of our industries and the jobs they provide. Basically, free trade is nothing short of the liberalization of Canadian and Quebec businesses.
Having been a member of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Canada's International Relations which, during the summer of 1985, held hearings throughout Canada on the possibility of concluding an agreement between our two countries, I can tell you that these hearings made us realize that most Canadians in all sectors of activities were in favour of such an agreement. We heard all groups and individuals anxious to give evidence- cloose to 300 witnesses. The hearings enabled us to find out what Canadians thought and wanted before our Government

June 21, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
undertook serious negotiations with the Americans, the negotiations which finally led to the agreement we are talking about today.
Throughout the hearings most witnesses invariably raised the issue of the very strong American protectionist trend which was a source of very deep Canadian concerns-and I need only refer to lumber, potash, chicken, just to name a few. In addition we ought to keep in mind the fact that, as I speak, 175 legislative measures and the famous omnibus bill-all protectionist initiatives-are pending before the American Congress and the Senate. We therefore had to act promptly to counter this protectionist movement which can be traced back to a number of factors, not the least of which is undoubtedly the slow and vacillating worldwide economic recovery after the recession of the early 1980s, and which is also due to the transition period now being experienced by the international economy.
The Free Trade Agreement therefore offsets and protects Canadians against these measures which Americans were advocating and would have continued to impose had the FTA not been signed.
The importance of trade relations between Canada and the United-States also concerned the Trudeau government, which set up, in 1982, the Royal Commission on Economic Union and Development Prospects. This Commission chaired by Donald Macdonald, former Liberal Cabinet minister costed Canadians 20 million dollars ... Its report, published in 1985, concluded that Canada had to negotiate a Free-Trade Agreement with the United-States.
Let me tell you what this important and voluminous report had to say on the matter: "The world offers Canada enormous challenges and opportunities. Jobs in Canada are threatened by the rapid growth of imports from developing countries, by changes in trade policies and by internal pressures on our trading partners in favour of new forms of protection. Inversely, the growth and technical progress in foreign countries open up new export opportunities and allow us to obtain cheaper and better goods.
Further on, the report says: "The pursuit of Canada-U.S. free trade is not at odds with efforts to strengthen and improve the existing multilateral framework. Rather, Commissionners see it as a complementary approach, involving concentration of our efforts and scarce resources on our most important market.
We see multilateral negotiations proceeding in parallel. In our view, such a two-tiered approach is the best way to ensure that Canadian industry will win sufficient acccess to foreign markets to invest and grow with confidence. At the same time, it will allow us to open our market in an orderly fashion and thus ensure that trade policy does its part in encouraging the development of a more competitive and more productive economy.
Following this introduction, here are the recommendations made in the Macdonald Commission Report: "Canada is
sufficiently strong and independent, however, to pursue bilateral initiatives, including better economic relations with the United States, within the framework of multilateral relations.
Commissioners recommend that the Government of Canada, at the same time it undertakes an initiative at the multilateral level to eliminate trade barriers, open negotiations with the Government of the United States to reach agreement on a substantial reduction of barriers, tariff and non-tariff, between Canada and the United States."
The report goes on to mention that "such an agreement would have to stand within the terms of article XXIV of GATT, protect Canadian culture and that an approach should be developed to use measures of contingent protection by establishing a new Canada-U.S. intergovernmental body to settle potential disputes."
That is what the Macdonald Report recommended.
To show that the free trade agreement is good for Quebec and Canada, and that the overall approach followed by this Government is successful, let us remember that Donald Macdonald, a previous member of the federal Cabinet and chairman of that Royal Inquiry, as well as Gerald Regan, the former Liberal Minister for External Trade, today are among its strongest supporters.
The free trade agreement opens to us Quebecers the door to futur success. And Quebecers have seen all the opportunities that agreement opens up for Quebec. Premier Robert Bourassa is a strong supporter, as well as the former Ministers of Finance Mr. Parizeau and Mr. Landry. Robert Campeau, one of our greatest Canadian entrepreneurs stated, and I quote:
Free trade is the single most important political action in Canada since the
turn of the century.
The chairman of Telemedia, Philippe de Gaspe Beaubien, stated:
That agreement is the key to our future prosperity and strength as a
country.
In Quebec we have shown our know-how over these last 30 years, both provincially, nationally and internatinally. Our confidence has led to major economic development and success stories like Hydro-Quebec, Bombardier ...

People are not going to buy our products because they like us but because they are high-quality products that are competitive on international markets. That has been Canada's strength in the past and will be in the future as well.
We must break out of our isolation and go out to conquer new markets. This is an appeal to collective excellence. We say to Canadians: Dare to be the best, and I have no doubts about how Canadians will respond to this appeal. We are people who like a challenge, especially Quebecers.
I am very concerned about the future of the science and technology sector, and I am convinced that our high-tech industries cannot survive without privileged access to U.S. markets. As the President of the Canadian Technology Association said so eloquently: "The market for computers, telecommunications and information technology is international, and if you don't aim for the international market, sooner or
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
later somebody else will come and wipe you out on your domestic market".
That is a harsh truth, Mr. Speaker. If we want to compete with the Americans, the Europeans and the Japanese, we need the basic elements of international competitiveness. The most critical factor for Canadians is to have free and secure access to the richest market on earth.
As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister responsible for Science and Technology, I am interested in research and development and the industrial applications of research. This Government, together with the provinces and all parties concerned, has for the first time in Canada's history developed a national policy on science and technology. The Prime Minister has taken an active part in preparing this policy and in the subsequent follow-up.
We know for a fact that Canada's great challenge is not scientific or technological research as such but the industrial applications of this research. Our businesses and high-tech industries must produce for a market of at least 100 million people to operate on a profitable a basis. This is just what the Free Trade Agreement offers us.
Before concluding my speech, I would like to talk about the impact of the Agreement on Canadian women. Mr. Speaker, I find deplorable the campaign of fear, if not terror, waged by some Opposition Members and union representatives. It is one thing, Mr. Speaker, to oppose a Government project. It is something else to lie knowingly to millions of women in order to terrorize them.
What are they telling Canadian women? That they will lose their jobs; that our health and welfare system will be destroyed; that the violence one finds in the streets of Detroit, New York or Miami will come to the streets of our great cities; that we will not be able to have child care facilities.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, one would have to be desperately cynical to wage such a campaign! We know, because we have the final text of the agreement, that all those statements are imaginary. Nothing in the agreement affects our health and welfare system. Nothing in the agreement threatens our social programs, including child care. Nothing in the agreement changes our Criminal Code, our legal system and our social values. I conclude, Mr. Speaker, it will not take too long ...
On the contrary, the Free Trade Agreement will help our economy grow more and create more jobs than ever. This means that we will have more wealth to distribute through our social programs. It also means that women will have better opportunities to pursue their careers or launch their own businesses.
I am proud of this great Bill introduced by the Government to implement the Accord and I intend to vote for it. It is a declaration by the people of Canada of their confidence, abilities and national maturity.
